title: Cancellation & Timeouts
scopeHtml: Scope: cooperative cancellation, cancellation checks, CancellationException semantics, swallowing cancellation, cleanup with NonCancellable, withTimeout/withTimeoutOrNull, timeout resource leaks, runInterruptible, Retrofit/OkHttp and Room behavior under cancellation. Facts checked against kotlinx.coroutines 1.8–1.10 docs. Exception propagation in general is covered in C6 and Job/scope structure in C4.

notes.title: Cooperative cancellation and cancellation points
notes.html:
The idea, simply. Cancelling a coroutine does not pull the plug. It raises a flag that says "please stop". The coroutine only stops when its own code looks at the flag. Like a teacher saying "pencils down": students must actually listen.

Mechanism. job.cancel() moves the Job to Cancelling (isActive == false). Nothing interrupts a running thread. The coroutine stops only at a cancellation point: a suspending function from kotlinx.coroutines that checks the Job and throws CancellationException if it is cancelled.

Cancellation points (check the flag for you). delay, yield, withContext, withTimeout, await, join, Channel.send/receive, Mutex.lock, Flow.emit/collect (emit checks ensureActive), anything built on suspendCancellableCoroutine.

Not cancellation points. Plain loops, blocking calls, Thread.sleep, regular IO streams, JSON parsing, bitmap decoding, a suspend function that never really suspends (suspend fun f() { heavyLoop() }).

// BUG: cancel() has no effect until the loop ends
val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
    var i = 0
    while (i < 1_000_000_000) { i = compute(i) }       // never checks the flag
}
job.cancel()    // job.isActive == false, but the CPU keeps burning

Production symptom. After leaving a screen, battery/CPU stays high; Perfetto shows DefaultDispatcher-worker busy; isActive is false on the leaked job. Fix by adding checks (next section) and splitting work into chunks.

Industry examples. Image pipelines (Coil/Glide decoding loops), Room query loops over huge cursors, Spotify-style local-library indexers, ML preprocessing loops on Dispatchers.Default: all must check cancellation so a scrolled-away item stops work.

Real-life picture. A road worker told by radio to stop: if he is wearing noise-cancelling headphones (a tight loop), he keeps digging.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing cancel() stops the thread. It never does.
  • Thinking a suspend keyword makes a function cancellable. Only real suspension points check.
  • Using Thread.sleep in a coroutine and wondering why cancel() waits.

notes.title: isActive, ensureActive and yield
notes.html:
Three ways to cooperate.

Tool What it does Throws? Cost
isActive boolean property in a CoroutineScope (reads the Job state) no a volatile read
ensureActive() throws CancellationException if cancelled yes same, tiny
yield() checks cancellation and lets other coroutines on the same dispatcher run yes dispatches, more expensive 
scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
    for (file in files) {
        ensureActive()               // stop promptly between items
        process(file)
    }
}
while (isActive) { step() }          // equivalent for loop conditions

Use ensureActive() when you only want to stop. Use yield() when you also want fairness (many CPU-heavy coroutines on a small dispatcher). isActive is for loop conditions or to run custom cleanup before leaving without throwing. Inside suspend functions that are not scope extensions use currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive().

Cost of checks (cost/perf scenario). A check is about one volatile read, so calling it every iteration of a 10 ns loop would be noticeable but typically negligible. Common pattern: check every N items or every chunk (for example every 256 rows or every ~10 ms), not on every byte. yield() costs a dispatch round-trip (hundreds of ns to microseconds), so never call it per item in a tight loop.

Industry example. Paging libraries and Room's generated code check cancellation between rows/batches; Jetpack Paging PagingSource.load relies on the coroutine being cancelled when the PagingData is dropped.

Real-life picture. A cashier glancing at the queue sign after each customer, not after each item scanned.

Common interview traps.

  • Checking isActive but then catching the exception and continuing.
  • Calling yield() on every iteration of a hot loop.
  • Using isActive inside a Thread {} (no scope there).

notes.title: CancellationException and swallowing
notes.html:
The idea. Cancellation is implemented as an exception: CancellationException (an IllegalStateException subclass in kotlinx.coroutines; on JVM it is java.util.concurrent.CancellationException). It is special: it does not crash the app, is not reported to the exception handler, and does not cancel the parent when thrown by a child. It is how a cancelled coroutine unwinds its stack, running finally blocks on the way out.

Swallowing it is a bug. If you catch it and carry on, the coroutine thinks it is alive and continues work after being cancelled.

// BUG 1: catches everything, including cancellation
try { api.fetch() } catch (e: Exception) { log(e) }
// BUG 2: runCatching has the same problem
val r = runCatching { api.fetch() }
// FIX
try { api.fetch() } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } catch (e: Exception) { log(e) }

Production incident (swallowed cancellation). A search box did viewModelScope.launch { try { results = repo.search(q) } catch (e: Exception) { showError() } } with collectLatest/cancel-on-new-query. Cancellation was caught as an error, so the stale request showed an error banner (or the old coroutine kept running and overwrote newer results). Symptoms: spurious error toasts, wrong final screen state, retry loops that never stop (retry wrapper catching Exception and trying again after cancellation, burning battery).

Foreign CancellationException. A CancellationException that comes from elsewhere, e.g. java.util.concurrent.CancellationException from a Future.get() or a cancelled third-party library/Retrofit call, does not mean your coroutine was cancelled. If you rethrow all CancellationExceptions blindly, you turn a library's cancelled future into a silent end of your coroutine; if you swallow them, you ignore real cancellation. Rule: check your own state: catch (e: CancellationException) { coroutineContext.ensureActive(); /* if still active it was foreign */ handle(e) }. ensureActive() rethrows if your Job is cancelled.

Rules of thumb.

  • Catch specific types (IOException, HttpException) instead of Exception/Throwable.
  • If you must catch Exception in suspend code, rethrow CancellationException first.
  • runCatching in suspend code needs the same care (many teams write a suspendRunCatching helper that rethrows it).
  • Throwing CancellationException from your own code is allowed; passing a message makes logs clearer.

Industry examples. Detekt rule SuspendFunSwallowedCancellation exists for exactly this; Google's Now in Android and Slack's code bases ship runCatching replacements.

Real-life picture. A fire alarm that a worker silences with a pillow: the building is still burning.

Common interview traps.

  • catch (e: Exception) or Throwable around suspend calls without rethrowing.
  • Using runCatching for suspend calls.
  • Assuming every CancellationException means the current coroutine was cancelled.

notes.title: finally cleanup and NonCancellable
notes.html:
The idea. When a coroutine is cancelled, its finally blocks still run: this is where you close files, release locks, unregister listeners. But the Job is already cancelled, so any suspending call inside finally throws CancellationException immediately (the first cancellation point).

try {
    work()
} finally {
    saveDraft()          // suspend fun: throws CancellationException at its first suspension!
}

Fix: withContext(NonCancellable) for short, essential cleanup:

try { work() } finally {
    withContext(NonCancellable) { saveDraft(); api.releaseLock() }
}

NonCancellable is a Job that is always active, so inside that block cancellation checks pass. Only valid with withContext (do not pass it to launch; that breaks the parent link and is the misuse pattern).

Misuse (spot-the-bug).

  • Wrapping the whole body in withContext(NonCancellable): now cancel() does nothing; screens leave, work continues.
  • Passing NonCancellable to launch(NonCancellable): detaches from the parent, so it is never cancelled and not tracked (a leak).
  • Doing long network calls (30 s) in the NonCancellable block: a cancelled Activity's work keeps running; combine with a timeout withTimeout(2_000) inside it.
  • Using it to "make a call survive screen exit": use an application scope or WorkManager instead.

Cancellation and side effects. If the coroutine is cancelled halfway, side effects already done stay done (written half a file, sent a request). Design for it: make writes atomic (write to temp then rename, Room transaction), make server calls idempotent (idempotency keys), and put compensating actions in finally (NonCancellable). Also remember that finally code that fails can hide the original exception (it becomes suppressed).

Industry examples. Room closing a cursor; OkHttp releasing connections; ExoPlayer releasing codecs; apps saving "last read position" in finally with NonCancellable when a chat screen closes (WhatsApp-style read markers).

Real-life picture. Even when the fire drill is on, you are allowed to lock the safe on the way out. But not allowed to start a new meeting.

Common interview traps.

  • Suspend calls in finally without NonCancellable.
  • Making the entire coroutine non-cancellable.
  • Using GlobalScope/NonCancellable as a "survive the screen" tool.

notes.title: Timeouts with withTimeout and TimeoutCancellationException
notes.html:
The idea. withTimeout(ms) { } runs the block and cancels it if it takes too long.

Function On timeout
withTimeout(t) throws TimeoutCancellationException
withTimeoutOrNull(t) returns null (the block's result type becomes nullable)

Semantics of TimeoutCancellationException. It is a subclass of CancellationException. Therefore:

  • Thrown inside the timed block, it cancels only that block; the outer coroutine is not cancelled, so it can catch it and continue.
  • If nobody catches it, it reaches the coroutine's boundary and is treated like a normal cancellation: no crash, nothing reported, the coroutine silently ends. This is a trap: uncaught timeouts disappear, causing "spinner forever / no error shown".
  • A generic catch (e: Exception) catches it too, so a timeout can be mistaken for "user cancelled" or swallowed (see the swallowing section). Prefer withTimeoutOrNull or catch TimeoutCancellationException explicitly (before CancellationException).
val data = withTimeoutOrNull(3_000) { api.load() } ?: return Result.Timeout
try { withTimeout(3_000) { api.load() } } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { showTimeout() }

There is also a Duration overload (withTimeout(3.seconds)).

Asynchronous timeout and resources. The timeout is delivered asynchronously: the block may have already produced a resource (an opened file, an acquired connection, a Bitmap) at the moment the timeout fires, and that value is then lost: the exception wins even if the block returned a hair earlier. The resource leaks unless you close it inside the block using try/finally or use {}.

withTimeout(2_000) {
    val conn = pool.acquire()
    try { conn.query() } finally { conn.release() }   // not outside the block!
}

Post-incident pattern. A payment SDK used withTimeout(5_000) { socket = connect(); handshake(socket) } and assigned socket to an outer variable closed only on success: each timeout leaked a socket; after hours, "too many open files" (FD limit ~1024 on many devices). Fix: acquire and release within the same block.

Industry examples. Retrofit/OkHttp already have call timeouts; withTimeout is used on top for overall deadlines (Uber-like "find a driver within 10 s"), splash-screen config fetch (Firebase Remote Config: withTimeoutOrNull(2s) then default values).

Real-life picture. A chess clock: when your time runs out the game for that move is over, but you may still walk away with the pieces you picked up.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking a timeout crashes the app (it does not, if uncaught it just vanishes).
  • Catching CancellationException first and treating timeout as user-cancel.
  • Releasing resources outside the timed block.
  • Timeout on blocking code (see the blocking section).

notes.title: cancel, cancelAndJoin and propagation
notes.html:
cancel vs cancelAndJoin. job.cancel() is a request and returns immediately; the Job is in Cancelling while finally blocks run. job.cancelAndJoin() cancels and then suspends until the job is complete. Use it when the next step depends on cleanup being done (closing the DB right after, replacing an old job with a new one using the same resource).

searchJob?.cancelAndJoin()    // wait for old cleanup
searchJob = scope.launch { ... }

Cancelling the parent. Cancel flows down to all children (each stops at its next cancellation point). A cancelled scope is permanently dead: new launch calls return a cancelled Job immediately and run nothing (the "nothing works after the error" bug). launch from a cancelled scope does not throw: it fails quietly.

Cancelling a child. Does not affect parent or siblings (it is a CancellationException). That's how withTimeout and collectLatest can cancel one operation safely.

Job states. Active, then Cancelling (waiting for finally and children), then Cancelled. isCompleted is true only at the end.

Cancel with a cause. job.cancel(CancellationException("user left")) makes diagnostics clearer; cancel() without a cause uses a generic one (JobCancellationException).

Real-life picture. Telling a taxi to stop vs waiting until the passenger is actually out of the car before you close the door.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming cancel() finished cleanup when it returns.
  • Reusing a scope after scope.cancel().
  • Thinking a child's cancellation cancels its parent.

notes.title: Blocking code and runInterruptible
notes.html:
The problem. withTimeout and cancel() only work at suspension points. A blocking call (Thread.sleep, socket.read(), queue.take(), Future.get(), a legacy Java SDK) never checks. So a timeout around blocking code does not interrupt it: withTimeout cannot resume until the blocked call returns (the coroutine is stuck in a non-cancellable section), which defeats the purpose.

withTimeout(1_000) { legacy.blockingFetch() }   // may take 30 s, timeout fires only afterwards

runInterruptible. Runs the block on Dispatchers.IO by default and, on cancellation, calls Thread.interrupt() on the thread. Blocking JDK calls that honour interrupts (Thread.sleep, BlockingQueue.take, Object.wait, NIO channels, Future.get) then throw InterruptedException, which runInterruptible converts to CancellationException.

withTimeout(1_000) { runInterruptible { legacy.blockingFetch() } }

Limits. Not everything honours interrupt: classic InputStream.read on a socket, java.io file reads, some native code, JDBC drivers. For those, close the underlying resource on cancellation (invokeOnCompletion/suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont.invokeOnCancellation { socket.close() } }). Android specifics: OkHttp has its own Call.cancel() (below).

Production incident. An SDK init wrapped in withTimeout(3s) still froze the splash screen for 15 s on poor networks because blockingConnect() was not interruptible; ANR-rate rose. Fix: move to Dispatchers.IO, use runInterruptible or the library's async API, and set the SDK's own socket timeouts.

Real-life picture. Shouting "stop" at someone wearing headphones works only if you tap them on the shoulder (interrupt), and some people still do not react.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing withTimeout forcibly kills blocking code.
  • Using runInterruptible on Dispatchers.Main.
  • Assuming every blocking call is interruptible.

notes.title: Retrofit OkHttp and Room cancellation
notes.html:
Retrofit/OkHttp. For suspend fun Retrofit service methods (Retrofit 2.6+), the adapter uses suspendCancellableCoroutine and call.enqueue(...); invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() }. So cancelling the coroutine cancels the HTTP call; OkHttp tears down the connection (HTTP/2 stream reset, HTTP/1.1 connection closed). The cancelled call throws IOException("Canceled") on its own thread; the coroutine machinery turns that into the CancellationException for you. Two consequences: the server may have already processed a POST (cancel does not undo side effects, so use idempotency keys), and an exception from a cancelled call can briefly show up as an IOException in your catch (so check ensureActive() before showing an error).

Room. suspend DAO methods run on Room's query/transaction executor. Room's coroutine support uses a CancellationSignal for queries (it cancels the SQLite statement in newer versions, so check your Room version) so a cancelled query can stop. For withTransaction { }: cancellation inside the block makes the transaction roll back (an exception ends it without setTransactionSuccessful), so you won't get half-applied writes, but only if you don't swallow the exception. A transaction block with NonCancellable inside is a smell. Be careful: inserting a row and then calling a network API inside the same transaction holds the DB lock (blocks other writers) and cancellation may arrive mid-way.

Industry examples. Search-as-you-type screens (Swiggy, Google Maps place search) cancel the previous request per keystroke via collectLatest/flatMapLatest; this relies on OkHttp cancellation to save bandwidth.

Real-life picture. Cancelling a taxi after the driver already left: the driver turns around (call cancelled), but you may still be charged (server side effect happened).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing cancel guarantees the server did not process the request.
  • Showing a network-error UI for an IOException("Canceled").
  • Using NonCancellable inside transactions to "protect" writes.

notes.title: Prompt cancellation guarantee
notes.html:
The idea. Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.4, functions like withContext, await and suspendCancellableCoroutine follow the prompt cancellation guarantee: if the Job is cancelled while the function is suspended, it throws CancellationException and never returns a value, even if the result was already computed.

val bmp = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { decode() }  // cancelled while decoding finishes?
// If cancelled at the moment decode() returned, withContext throws; the result is dropped
imageView.setImageBitmap(bmp)     // not reached

Why it matters. Safety for UI: you never touch a destroyed screen with a stale result after leaving. Cost: the dropped result may hold a resource (Bitmap, cursor, file) that you will not receive and cannot close. Close inside the block, or return a wrapper whose cleanup you do via invokeOnCancellation / onUndeliveredElement (for channels).

For your own suspendCancellableCoroutine. Resume once; register invokeOnCancellation { cancelSource() }; if the continuation was cancelled before your callback fires, resume is ignored (resume(value) { cause -> release(value) } overload with onCancellation lets you release it).

Real-life picture. A parcel arrives after you cancelled the order: it goes straight back to the warehouse; you never get to see it.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting a result after cancellation just because it was computed.
  • Leaking resources returned by a cancelled withContext.
  • Calling resume twice in suspendCancellableCoroutine.

notes.title: Cancellation in Flow collection
notes.html:
The idea. Collecting a flow is a suspend call running in the collector's coroutine, so cancelling that coroutine cancels the flow. flow { } builders check cancellation on each emit (ensureActive is called inside emit), so a collector that stops stops the producer on the next emit.

Gotchas.

  • A CPU-bound flow { while(true) { emit(compute()) } } stops at the emit. But a long loop without emit never checks: add ensureActive() or use .cancellable() on flows built from asFlow()/sharedFlow (some operators like asFlow() on collections check automatically in recent versions; .cancellable() makes sure).
  • collectLatest { } cancels the previous block when a new value arrives; that block receives CancellationException, so don't swallow it.
  • catch { } operator does not catch downstream exceptions or cancellation; it handles upstream failures only. A try/catch(Exception) around collect swallows cancellation.
  • launchIn(scope) and viewModelScope flows end with the scope; in UI use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) so collection is cancelled when the screen is in the background and restarted on return (collection is not just paused: the upstream is cancelled, saving battery/location updates).
  • callbackFlow { awaitClose { unregister() } }: awaitClose runs on cancellation; without it you leak the callback.

Real-life picture. A tap that stops running when the bucket is taken away.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting awaitClose in callbackFlow.
  • Catching Exception around collect and swallowing cancellation.
  • Assuming flowOn or .catch change who can cancel.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Cancellation is cooperative: cancel() sets a flag; only cancellation points (delay, yield, withContext, await, emit...) or explicit ensureActive()/isActive checks stop work.
  • CancellationException is the mechanism; never swallow it (catch (Exception), runCatching); rethrow it, or catch specific exceptions. Beware foreign CancellationExceptions.
  • finally runs on cancel, but suspend calls there fail unless wrapped in withContext(NonCancellable), kept short. Never make the whole coroutine non-cancellable.
  • TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException; it cancels only the timed block, silently ends the coroutine if uncaught, and the result may be dropped, so release resources inside the block.
  • Blocking code ignores withTimeout; use runInterruptible (interruptible calls only) or close the resource.
  • Retrofit cancels OkHttp calls on cancellation but server effects may remain; Room transactions roll back on cancellation.
  • Prompt cancellation guarantee: a cancelled withContext/await never returns its result.
  • Flow collection cancels with the collector; use repeatOnLifecycle, awaitClose, ensureActive.

questions.promptHtml: What does it mean that coroutine cancellation is "cooperative"? What actually happens when I call job.cancel()?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates think cancel() kills the coroutine the way Thread.stop() would. This question tests whether they know cancellation is a flag that the code itself has to observe.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: job.cancel() doesn't stop any code. It flips the Job into a cancelling state and records a CancellationException as the cause. The coroutine only reacts the next time it reaches a cancellation point: a cancellable suspending call like delay, withContext, await or Channel.receive, or an explicit check like ensureActive(). At that point it throws CancellationException, which unwinds the stack through finally blocks. Code that never suspends and never checks keeps running to the end. That is what "cooperative" means.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A coroutine is just code running on some thread. The library can't safely stop a thread halfway through an instruction. The JVM gave that up when Thread.stop() was deprecated, because it left locks and invariants corrupted. So kotlinx.coroutines uses the same model as Thread.interrupt(): set a flag and let the code notice it.

What cancel() does, step by step:

  1. The Job's state moves from Active to Cancelling. isActive becomes false and isCancelled becomes true. isCompleted stays false.
  2. A CancellationException (internally a JobCancellationException with a message like "StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled") is stored as the cancellation cause.
  3. Every child Job is cancelled too, recursively.
  4. If the coroutine is currently suspended in a cancellable suspension, such as one built on suspendCancellableCoroutine (delay, await, join, channel ops, Retrofit suspend calls), it is resumed right away with that exception. Any invokeOnCancellation handlers run, for example OkHttp's call.cancel().
  5. If the coroutine is running right now on a thread, nothing happens until it reaches its next cancellation point.
  6. Once the body has finished unwinding and all children have completed, the Job moves to Cancelled, which is a final state with isCompleted = true.
 cancel()            body throws CE / finishes      all children done
Active ───────► Cancelling ──────────────────────────────► Cancelled
 isActive=true   isActive=false, isCancelled=true          isCompleted=true

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: never observes cancellation; runs the full 5 seconds of CPU work
val job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
    var x = 0L
    val end = System.currentTimeMillis() + 5_000
    while (System.currentTimeMillis() < end) x++   // no suspension, no check
}
job.cancel() // returns immediately; the loop keeps burning a Default thread

// Correct: cooperative
val job2 = scope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
    var x = 0L
    while (isActive) x++           // or ensureActive() inside the loop
}
job2.cancelAndJoin()               // (from a suspend context) returns once the loop has actually exited

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming cancel() is synchronous. It returns before the coroutine has stopped. Use cancelAndJoin() if you need to wait.
  • Assuming Thread.sleep, blocking IO or a JNI call is interrupted. They are not.
  • Thinking cancellation "fails" the parent. A cancelled child does not cancel its parent. Cancellation flows down the tree, not up.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is job.cancel() thread-safe? → Yes. Job state is updated with lock-free atomics, so you can call it from any thread.
  2. What if I cancel a coroutine that hasn't started yet? → With the default CoroutineStart.DEFAULT, the body may never run, including its try/finally. Only ATOMIC/UNDISPATCHED guarantee the body starts (see C2).
  3. Why not just interrupt the thread? → Coroutines share pooled threads. Interrupting one would hit whatever coroutine happens to run on it next. runInterruptible makes that safe in a bounded scope (Q364).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "cancel stops the coroutine, use isActive". The senior answer walks through the Cancelling → Cancelled states, explains that cancellable suspensions resume immediately while running code only notices at checkpoints, and points out that cleanup and children still finish before the Job completes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team found image-processing jobs still pegging all 8 Default threads after the user left the screen. The filters were pure CPU loops with no checks, so the next screen's work was starved.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between isActive, ensureActive() and yield()? When would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They want to see whether you know the three ways to make non-suspending code cancellable, and the cost and semantics of each.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: All three check the Job. isActive is a boolean read with no side effects, so I use it as a loop condition when I want to exit gracefully and maybe return a partial result. ensureActive() throws CancellationException if the Job isn't active, so it behaves like any other cancellation point and unwinds through finally. yield() is a real suspension point: it checks for cancellation, and on a dispatcher that needs dispatching it also gives the thread to other coroutines waiting on it. I use it when a long CPU task must stay fair on a shared, limited pool.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API Suspends? On cancellation Extra effect Cost
isActive (CoroutineScope / CoroutineContext ext) No returns false none volatile read
ensureActive() No throws job.getCancellationException() none volatile read + branch
yield() Yes throws CE re-dispatches, letting other coroutines on the same dispatcher run allocation + dispatch, microseconds

Details that matter:

  • isActive inside a suspend function with no scope receiver: use currentCoroutineContext().isActive, or coroutineContext.isActive. Inside a flow {} builder, currentCoroutineContext() is the safe choice because the coroutineContext name can resolve to the wrong receiver in some lambdas.
  • ensureActive() throws the same exception the Job was cancelled with, so a custom cause such as cancel("user logged out") keeps its message.
  • yield() on Dispatchers.Default really gives the thread to queued coroutines. That matters when 8 cores are shared by dozens of CPU tasks. On a single-threaded dispatcher such as Main, it lets other queued tasks run first.
  • A while (isActive) loop exits normally. Code after the loop runs and the coroutine completes as cancelled, because its Job was cancelled, but no exception unwinds your stack. That's useful for "return what you have so far". It's dangerous if callers assume a normal return means the work is complete.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun hashAll(files: List<File>): Map<File, String> = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    val out = HashMap<File, String>(files.size)
    for (f in files) {
        ensureActive()                 // throw promptly between items
        out[f] = sha256(f)             // CPU-bound, non-suspending
    }
    out
}

// Graceful partial result using isActive
suspend fun searchLocal(query: String, items: List<Item>): List<Item> = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    val hits = ArrayList<Item>()
    for (item in items) {
        if (!isActive) break           // caller cancelled; the partial list is thrown away anyway (see note)
        if (item.matches(query)) hits += item
    }
    hits
}

Note: in the second example, withContext throws CancellationException on return anyway, because its caller is cancelled and it has a prompt cancellation guarantee (Q368). So the "partial result" never reaches a cancelled caller. isActive partial results only make sense when the loop's own coroutine keeps running, for example a loop with its own exit policy.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling yield() on every iteration of a 1M-item loop. The dispatch overhead can make it several times slower (see Q375). Check every N items or every few milliseconds instead.
  • Using Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted. That has nothing to do with coroutine cancellation.
  • Expecting isActive to throw. It doesn't, so a while (isActive) loop followed by "save result" will save a partial result.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does delay(0) check cancellation? → Don't rely on it. In the kotlinx.coroutines source, delay with a non-positive time returns immediately, before reaching the cancellable suspension, so it is not a checkpoint. Use ensureActive() or yield(), which state the intent anyway.
  2. Is ensureActive() available on a Job directly? → Yes, Job.ensureActive(), alongside the CoroutineScope and CoroutineContext extensions.
  3. How does yield() behave on Dispatchers.Unconfined? → It still checks cancellation, but there is no real thread to give up. Unconfined has special yield handling, so don't rely on fairness there.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "they all check cancellation". The senior answer separates the graceful exit (isActive), the exceptional exit (ensureActive) and fairness (yield), knows yield costs a dispatch, and knows withContext discards partial results anyway.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team added yield() to every row of a 200k-row CSV import "to be safe" and made the import roughly 3x slower. Switching to ensureActive() every 1,000 rows restored the speed with no loss in cancellation latency.

questions.promptHtml: What is CancellationException in coroutines, and why doesn't an uncaught one crash the app the way other exceptions do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Almost every cancellation bug comes from not understanding that cancellation is delivered as an exception that the machinery treats as a normal outcome.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cancellation is delivered as a CancellationException thrown at a cancellation point, so finally blocks and use {} run as the stack unwinds. On the JVM it's a typealias for java.util.concurrent.CancellationException. The coroutine machinery treats it as normal completion of a cancelled coroutine, not as a failure. It doesn't cancel the parent, it isn't passed to a CoroutineExceptionHandler, and it doesn't reach the thread's uncaught exception handler, which is why it never crashes the app. Any other exception means failure: it cancels the parent and, at the root, crashes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
When a coroutine's body completes with a throwable, its Job asks: is this a CancellationException?

  • Yes: the Job finishes as Cancelled. The parent gets a notification that the child completed, but is not cancelled. Nothing is reported.
  • No: the Job fails. It cancels its parent with this exception as the cause, the failure propagates up, and at the root, launch hands it to a CoroutineExceptionHandler or the thread's uncaught exception handler, which crashes on Android. Details are in C6.
throwable from body
      │
      ├── is CancellationException ──► Job = Cancelled, parent untouched, silent
      │
      └── other Throwable ──► Job = Failed ──► cancel parent ──► ... ──► root handler / crash

Why use an exception at all? Because unwinding through try/finally is the only way to give every frame on the (virtual) stack a chance to clean up: close a cursor, release a lock, delete a temp file. A boolean flag can't do that.

Subtypes you'll meet:

  • JobCancellationException (internal): thrown by ensureActive, delay, etc. after cancel(). Message: "Job was cancelled" / "StandaloneCoroutine was cancelled".
  • TimeoutCancellationException (public): from withTimeout (Q362).
  • Internal flow abort exceptions: first(), take() and similar use a CancellationException subclass internally to stop the upstream early. That's why catching CE inside a flow collector can break first().

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
scope.launch {
    try {
        repo.sync()                      // suspends; cancelled here
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        log("sync cancelled: ${e.message}")
        throw e                          // ALWAYS rethrow
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        showError(e)
    } finally {
        progress.hide()                  // non-suspending cleanup runs either way
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting CancellationException to Crashlytics as a non-fatal. It floods the dashboard with "Job was cancelled" noise and hides real errors.
  • Catching it and not rethrowing (Q360).
  • Throwing CancellationException yourself as control flow, for example "throw CancellationException to stop". That silently kills the coroutine in a way that looks like cancellation but isn't (Q367).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does CoroutineExceptionHandler see CE? → No. The handler is only invoked for failures, and CE is ignored by design.
  2. What happens if async is cancelled and someone calls await()? → await() throws CancellationException in the awaiting coroutine (Q367 covers why that's dangerous).
  3. Can cancellation have a non-CE cause? → job.cancel(cause) only takes a CancellationException. The internal cancel(Throwable) that marks a job as failed exists but is not public API. A child failing with a real exception cancels the parent with that exception as the cause, and siblings then see a CE whose cause chain contains it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it's thrown when you cancel, you should rethrow it". The senior answer explains how completion is classified (cancelled vs failed), why it doesn't propagate up or crash, the internal uses inside Flow, and the operational effect: never log it as an error.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: In one app, 40% of all Crashlytics non-fatals were JobCancellationExceptions from a blanket catch (e: Exception) { crashlytics.recordException(e) } in a base repository. The real network errors were buried under them.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between withTimeout and withTimeoutOrNull, and how does each signal a timeout?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a basic API question, but follow-ups quickly reach the fact that timeouts are cancellation, not a separate mechanism.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Both run a suspending block and cancel it if it exceeds the time limit. withTimeout then throws TimeoutCancellationException, which is a subclass of CancellationException. withTimeoutOrNull catches its own timeout and returns null. Since a timeout is just cancellation, the block only stops at cancellation points, so withTimeout around blocking code does nothing. I prefer withTimeoutOrNull when a timeout is an expected outcome, because a thrown TCE inside a launch silently ends the coroutine instead of failing it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism: withTimeout(t) starts the block in a child coroutine-like scope and schedules a delayed action on the dispatcher's Delay implementation (a Handler on Main, the scheduler on Default/IO). When it fires, that action cancels the block with a TimeoutCancellationException("Timed out waiting for t ms"). The block unwinds like any cancellation. Then:

Block finishes in time Block times out
withTimeout returns block result throws TimeoutCancellationException
withTimeoutOrNull returns block result (can be null itself) returns null

Both take Long milliseconds or a kotlin.time.Duration. Non-positive time means an immediate timeout.

Why TCE being a CE matters:

  • Inside launch { withTimeout(1000) { ... } }, an unhandled TCE makes the launch complete as cancelled. No crash, no handler, no log. The "operation timed out" signal disappears.
  • Inside runBlocking or coroutineScope, the exception is rethrown to the caller, which is why the docs' example prints a stack trace.
  • withTimeoutOrNull is ambiguous if the block can legitimately return null. Wrap the result (Result, a sealed type) if you need to distinguish.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Expected outcome -> OrNull + explicit handling
suspend fun fetchConfigOrDefault(): Config =
    withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { api.config() } ?: Config.DEFAULT

// Need a distinct error to surface: convert TCE to a domain failure
suspend fun loadProfile(): Result<Profile> = try {
    Result.success(withTimeout(5_000) { api.profile() })
} catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) {
    Result.failure(ProfileTimeout(e))    // not a CE anymore; a real error the UI can show
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping Thread.sleep / a blocking SDK in withTimeout and expecting it to fire (Q372).
  • Catching CancellationException in that try instead of TimeoutCancellationException. That also swallows the outer cancellation of the caller.
  • Treating null from withTimeoutOrNull as "timed out" when the block can return null.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does withTimeout use real time in runTest? → No. It uses the test scheduler's virtual time, so timeouts fire immediately when virtual time advances (see T1).
  2. Can withTimeout time out after the block has produced its value? → Yes. Cancellation is asynchronous, which causes the resource-leak pitfall (Q366).
  3. Is OkHttp's callTimeout equivalent? → Similar effect, different layer. OkHttp's timeout fails the call with InterruptedIOException, an IOException and not a CE, which makes it a normal error you can catch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "one throws, one returns null". The senior answer explains that a timeout is cancellation scheduled on the dispatcher's Delay, that a TCE silently ends a launch, how to convert it into a domain error, and the null ambiguity.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A splash screen used launch { withTimeout(3000) { warmUp() } ; navigate() }. On slow devices the TCE cancelled the launch, navigate() never ran, and users were stuck on the splash with nothing in the logs.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between job.cancel() and job.cancelAndJoin()? Walk me through isActive, isCancelled and isCompleted during cancellation.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether you know cancellation takes time and that "cancelled" is not the same as "done", which matters for restart logic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: cancel() only requests cancellation and returns immediately. cancelAndJoin() requests it and then suspends until the Job has actually completed, meaning its finally blocks and children are finished. While the Job is cancelling, isActive is false and isCancelled is true, but isCompleted is still false. isCompleted only becomes true once everything has unwound. If I'm about to restart the same work, for example writing the same file, I use cancelAndJoin() so the old and new runs never overlap.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
State isActive isCancelled isCompleted When
New (LAZY not started) false false false start = LAZY before start()
Active true false false running or suspended
Cancelling false true false after cancel(), unwinding, children finishing
Cancelled false true true final
Completing true false false body done, waiting for children
Completed false false true final, success

join() suspends until isCompleted. It does not throw if the target was cancelled. It does throw if the caller is cancelled while waiting, because join is itself a cancellable suspension. cancelAndJoin() is simply cancel(); join().

Why overlap happens: during Cancelling, the old coroutine may still be running a CPU stretch until its next check, or running a withContext(NonCancellable) cleanup that writes to disk. If you start the replacement immediately, both run at once.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Exporter(private val scope: CoroutineScope) {
    private var job: Job? = null

    fun restart(target: File) {
        val previous = job
        job = scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
            previous?.cancelAndJoin()     // old run fully unwound (temp file deleted) before we start
            export(target)
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Checking job.isCompleted straight after cancel() and treating false as an error.
  • if (job?.isActive == true) return as a "don't double-start" guard. During Cancelling it's false, so a second run starts while the first is still cleaning up.
  • Calling cancelAndJoin() on the coroutine you are inside, or on an ancestor. The job can't complete while you're waiting inside it. Cancellation usually rescues you, because join is cancellable and the CE breaks the wait, but the code is wrong and confusing. Cancel yourself with cancel() or throw, never with join.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does join() rethrow the job's failure? → No. join never rethrows. Deferred.await() does.
  2. How do I know why it was cancelled? → job.invokeOnCompletion { cause -> } gets null for success, a CE for cancellation, or the failure exception.
  3. Can a Cancelling job start new children? → launch on a cancelled scope creates a child that is cancelled immediately. With default start its body never runs (Q370).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "cancelAndJoin waits". The senior answer gives the full state table, explains why isActive is a bad overlap guard, shows a restart pattern with cancelAndJoin, and mentions invokeOnCompletion for the cause.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "regenerate thumbnail" button that called cancel() and immediately relaunched let two writers race on the same cache file. About 1 in 500 thumbnails came out corrupt until the code switched to cancelAndJoin().

questions.contextHtml:
A photo editor applies filters to a 12 MP image (4000x3000 = 12M pixels) on Dispatchers.Default. When users drag a slider, each change cancels the previous job and starts a new one. On a Pixel 6 (8 cores) it's fine. On low-end 4-core devices, about 30% of the user base, sliders feel frozen for 2–3 s and the "Save" button (also on Default) doesn't respond. Profiling shows all 4 Default workers busy running applyFilter. A teammate suspects GC pressure from bitmap allocation.

class FilterViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private var filterJob: Job? = null

    fun onSliderChanged(value: Float) {
        filterJob?.cancel()
        filterJob = viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
            val pixels = sourcePixels.copyOf()           // IntArray(12_000_000)
            for (i in pixels.indices) {
                pixels[i] = adjust(pixels[i], value)     // pure math
            }
            withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { preview.setPixels(pixels) }
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong, and how would you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Dispatchers.IO because it has more threads" or "it's GC, reuse the array". Moving to IO just hides CPU starvation behind 64 threads, and the GC theory is a red herring. Neither touches the actual bug: cancelled jobs keep running to completion.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How long does one full pass take on a low-end device? (It sets the scale of the waste.) How many slider events per second? (It tells me how many zombie passes pile up.) Does "Save" share Default? (It explains the frozen button.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a cancellation check to the loop. That's a one-line fix I'd ship as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The loop has no cancellation point. cancel() marks the job, but the 12M-iteration loop runs to the end, so every slider tick adds a full pass. At about 60 events/s and 300 ms per pass on a slow core, the 4 workers saturate within the first 100 ms. Most likely.
    • (b) GC from the 48 MB copyOf() per event (12M × 4 bytes). It's real, but it's secondary. It shows up as GC pauses, not as busy workers.
    • (c) The Main hop is slow. Unlikely, because the profile shows the workers inside applyFilter.
  4. How I'd verify each: A Perfetto trace shows DefaultDispatcher-worker-1..4 all in adjust for seconds after the slider stops. Adding CoroutineName("filter-$value") plus -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug shows several "cancelling" coroutines still running. The Memory profiler / GC events confirm (b) as secondary.
  5. Root cause: Cancellation is cooperative. Nothing in the loop suspends or checks the Job, so cancelled coroutines stay in the Cancelling state and hold a Default thread until the loop ends. Dispatchers.Default has only as many threads as cores (4 here), so "Save" is starved.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: check every N pixels, not every pixel.
    filterJob = viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
    val pixels = sourcePixels.copyOf()
    for (i in pixels.indices) {
        if (i and 0xFFFF == 0) ensureActive()   // every 65,536 px ≈ 183 checks per pass
        pixels[i] = adjust(pixels[i], value)
    }
    withContext(Dispatchers.Main) { preview.setPixels(pixels) }
}
    • Long term: conflate slider input (a MutableStateFlow + collectLatest / mapLatest, see F3/F4) so at most one pass runs. Reuse two pixel buffers to kill the 48 MB allocation per tick. Render a downscaled preview (1000x750 is 16x fewer pixels) while dragging and full resolution on release.
  7. Prevention: A code review checklist item: "any loop over more than 10k items or longer than 16 ms in a coroutine has a cancellation check". A unit test that cancels mid-run and asserts the job completes within 50 ms using cancelAndJoin with a timeout.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't call ensureActive() on every pixel (12M volatile reads, measurable but small) and definitely not yield() per pixel (12M dispatches). I wouldn't move CPU work to IO, which oversubscribes the CPU and starves IO tasks. I wouldn't use a single-thread dispatcher just to serialize, because conflation is the right tool.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if adjust is a JNI call that takes 2 s per call? → Checks between calls can't interrupt native code. Pass a cancel flag (an AtomicBoolean set from invokeOnCompletion) into the native loop, or split the native work into tiles.
  • Is isActive better than ensureActive here? → ensureActive is better. It throws and skips the Main hop. With isActive + break, we'd still post a half-processed image unless we check again.
  • Why did the Pixel 6 hide it? → 8 workers and a pass 3x faster meant zombies finished before they could saturate the pool.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: On a video-thumbnail strip, each scroll cancelled and relaunched frame extraction with no cancellation checks. On 4-core devices, 20 zombie decodes ran at once. One ensureActive() per frame cut CPU time during fast scroll by about 70%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames GC or suggests IO; doesn't know cancellation is cooperative.
  • Hire: adds ensureActive()/isActive and explains why the loop ignored cancel.
  • Strong hire: also batches the checks, explains Default's core-sized pool and starvation of "Save", proposes conflation and buffer reuse, and adds a test.

questions.promptHtml: Is every suspend function a cancellation point? Which calls are cancellable and which are not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates often believe that the suspend modifier makes code cancellable. It doesn't. Cancellability comes from how the suspension is implemented.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. suspend only means the function may suspend. A function is a cancellation point only if it suspends through a cancellable primitive like suspendCancellableCoroutine, or explicitly checks the Job. All the kotlinx.coroutines suspending functions are cancellable: delay, yield, withContext, await, join, channel ops, Mutex.lock. Retrofit and Room suspend calls are too. But a suspend function that just runs blocking code, or one built on plain suspendCoroutine, ignores cancellation until it returns.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A suspension is "cancellable" when the continuation is registered with the Job so that cancel() can resume it early with a CE. suspendCancellableCoroutine does that registration. suspendCoroutine doesn't, so cancelling while suspended there has no effect until whoever holds the continuation resumes it.

Call Cancellable? Notes
delay, yield, awaitCancellation Yes throw CE immediately when cancelled
withContext(ctx) Yes checks on entry; prompt cancellation guarantee on exit (Q368)
Deferred.await, Job.join Yes the caller's cancellation, not the target's
Channel.send/receive, Flow.collect emission suspensions Yes
Mutex.lock, Semaphore.acquire Yes
Retrofit suspend (2.6+) Yes invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() } (Q365)
Room suspend DAO Yes (at the dispatch boundary) a running SQLite statement may or may not abort (Q369)
suspendCoroutine { } wrappers No stuck until the callback resumes
Thread.sleep, blocking InputStream.read, Future.get() without timeout No blocking; use runInterruptible (Q364)
A suspend fun with only CPU code inside No no suspension ever happens
withContext(NonCancellable) body No (by design)

The compiler doesn't help here. suspend fun parse(json: String) = gson.fromJson(...) compiles fine, carries the suspend marker, and has zero cancellation points.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Not cancellable: suspend marker, but nothing to observe cancellation
suspend fun legacyFetch(): Data = suspendCoroutine { cont ->
    sdk.fetch { cont.resume(it) }          // cancel() is ignored; sdk keeps running and we stay suspended
}

// Cancellable
suspend fun fetch(): Data = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    val handle = sdk.fetch { cont.resume(it) }
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { handle.cancel() }
}

(Wrapping callbacks in depth belongs to C10. Here the point is only which side observes cancellation.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "it's a suspend fun so it's cancellable" in a code review.
  • Thinking await() cancels the Deferred. Cancelling the awaiting coroutine only stops the waiting. The async is cancelled only because it's usually a child of the same scope.
  • Forgetting that a cancelled coroutine can still enter a non-cancellable stretch and run for seconds.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. If a coroutine is cancelled before withContext is even called, does the block run? → No. withContext checks the resulting context and throws CE immediately, possibly without scheduling the block.
  2. Is Flow.collect cancellable if the flow never emits? → Only if the upstream suspends cancellably. A flow { while (true) compute() } with no suspension isn't.
  3. How do I find non-cancellable suspend functions in a big codebase? → Lint/grep for suspendCoroutine and blocking calls inside suspend (Android Studio's "Inappropriate blocking method call" inspection), plus cancellation tests that assert completion time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "suspend functions check cancellation". The senior answer says cancellability is a property of the suspension primitive, names suspendCoroutine and blocking calls as holes, and explains that await cancels the waiter, not the work.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A payment SDK wrapper used suspendCoroutine. Cancelled checkout screens left coroutines suspended forever, each pinning a Fragment through its continuation. LeakCanary flagged them after about 10 checkout attempts.

questions.promptHtml: Why are catch (e: Exception) and runCatching dangerous inside coroutines? What's the correct pattern?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common real-world cancellation bug, and it shows up in nearly every Android codebase.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CancellationException is an Exception (it's IllegalStateException → RuntimeException on the JVM), so a catch-all or runCatching, which catches Throwable, catches the cancellation signal too. If you don't rethrow it, the coroutine thinks it recovered. It keeps running past the point where it should have stopped, often looping or writing state for a screen that no longer exists. The fix is to rethrow CE before handling anything else, or to call ensureActive() in the catch block. For Result-style code I use a runSuspendCatching helper that rethrows CE.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
What actually happens when you swallow it:

  1. The Job is still marked cancelled. Swallowing the exception doesn't un-cancel the Job.
  2. Your code continues. The next cancellable suspension, such as delay, throws CE again immediately. So in a while (true) { try { work() } catch (e: Exception) { log(e) }; delay(5000) } loop, the catch eats the CE thrown by work(), the delay throws again, and the loop finally exits. That case usually self-heals by luck.
  3. It breaks badly when the next suspension sits inside the try, or when there is non-suspending work after the catch: catch (e: Exception) { _state.value = Error(e) } puts an error state on screen, or db.insert(failedRecord) runs from a blocking DAO. Then you get spurious "Error: Job was cancelled" UI states, analytics noise, and wasted work.
  4. With runCatching, the Result.failure(CancellationException) flows into .onFailure { showError() } or .getOrElse { fallback }, and the cancelled coroutine happily continues with a fallback value.

Correct patterns:

// 1) Rethrow first
try {
    api.upload(item)
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
} catch (e: Exception) {
    reportError(e)
}

// 2) ensureActive() in a catch-all (also catches foreign CEs correctly, see Q367)
try {
    api.upload(item)
} catch (e: Exception) {
    currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()   // rethrows if WE are cancelled
    reportError(e)
}

// 3) Result helper (not in stdlib; common team utility)
suspend inline fun <T> runSuspendCatching(block: () -> T): Result<T> =
    try {
        Result.success(block())
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e
    } catch (e: Throwable) {
        Result.failure(e)
    }

Why version 2 can be better than version 1: version 1 rethrows any CE, including a CE thrown by await() on someone else's cancelled Deferred while we are still active. Version 2 rethrows only when our Job is cancelled and treats a foreign CE as an ordinary error. Pick based on intent (Q367).

There's a long-standing request on the kotlinx.coroutines issue tracker (#1814) for a cancellation-aware runCatching. As of 1.10 there is no official one, so teams write their own.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (e: Throwable) in a base UseCase/Repository. It swallows cancellation for every call in the app.
  • Logging CE to Crashlytics as an error (Q355).
  • catch (e: Exception) { emit(Error) } inside a flow {}. That also violates exception transparency (F1/F6), but the cancellation side is our concern here.
  • Catching TimeoutCancellationException broadly as CancellationException, which swallows outer cancellation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a catch-all ever fine? → At a root boundary where the coroutine is about to finish anyway, swallowing is harmless. But "harmless here" rots in refactors, so rethrow consistently.
  2. Does Detekt/lint catch this? → Detekt has rules against swallowed exceptions in general, and there are community rules for coroutines. Many teams add a custom rule that flags runCatching inside suspend functions.
  3. What about Flow.catch {}? → catch doesn't intercept cancellation of the collector. Downstream cancellation isn't delivered to it. It's designed to be cancellation-safe.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "rethrow CancellationException". The senior answer explains that the Job stays cancelled so the next suspension rethrows, shows where it still does damage, gives the ensureActive() variant, and explains why it distinguishes own and foreign CEs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync loop wrapped in runCatching { }.onFailure { retryLater() } kept rescheduling WorkManager jobs every time its CoroutineWorker was stopped by the system. That produced about 30k redundant work requests per day across the fleet.

questions.promptHtml: What happens if I call a suspend function in a finally block of a cancelled coroutine? How and when should I use NonCancellable?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cleanup that silently never runs is a classic source of leaked resources and inconsistent state.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The finally block runs, but the coroutine is already cancelled, so the first cancellable suspension inside it throws CancellationException and the rest of the cleanup is skipped. Plain non-suspending cleanup like close() is fine. If cleanup has to suspend, for example telling the server or writing a "failed" row through a suspend DAO, I wrap just that part in withContext(NonCancellable) { }. NonCancellable is only for short cleanup and only with withContext. It's not for launch, and not for making a whole operation unkillable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
NonCancellable is a singleton Job that is always active and can't be cancelled. When withContext(NonCancellable) merges it into the context, it replaces the current Job, so code inside sees isActive == true and suspensions don't throw. Remember that the outer coroutine is still cancelled. Once the block returns, the next suspension outside it throws again.

launch {                        Job = J (cancelled)
  try { ... } finally {
    analytics.send()            ◄── throws CE immediately (J cancelled); rest of finally skipped
    withContext(NonCancellable) {   Job = NonCancellable (always active)
      analytics.send()          ◄── runs to completion
    }
  }
}

Rules:

  • Use it only with withContext. The docs say it's not designed for launch/async. launch(NonCancellable) creates a coroutine with no parent (NonCancellable has no children tracking), so it escapes structured concurrency: it isn't cancelled with the scope and isn't awaited by it.
  • Keep it short and bounded. A hung network call inside NonCancellable can't be cancelled at all, so add withTimeout inside it (a timeout still works there, because withTimeout creates its own cancellable child).
  • Don't combine it with a dispatcher change carelessly. The withContext docs warn that adding dispatcher-changing elements to the NonCancellable pattern can make the cleanup incorrect: the return path re-dispatches and the prompt-cancellation check can discard the result. Do the dispatcher switch inside, or rely on main-safe suspend APIs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun uploadWithCleanup(file: File) {
    val sessionId = api.startUpload(file.name)
    try {
        api.uploadChunks(sessionId, file)          // cancellable
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        withContext(NonCancellable) {
            withTimeoutOrNull(2_000) { api.abortUpload(sessionId) }  // bounded best-effort
        }
        throw e
    } finally {
        file.delete()                              // non-suspending: no NonCancellable needed
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping the whole operation in withContext(NonCancellable) "so it isn't interrupted". The screen leaves, and the work, its memory and the captured references live on (Q377).
  • launch(NonCancellable) { save() } as a "fire and forget save". Use an app-level scope or WorkManager (C7).
  • Forgetting that finally doesn't run at all if the coroutine was cancelled before it started (default start).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does use {} work for cleanup in coroutines? → Yes. close() is non-suspending, so use runs it during CE unwinding. use exists for Closeable/AutoCloseable.
  2. Is withContext(NonCancellable) cancellable by withTimeout inside it? → Yes. The timeout's child is cancellable relative to itself, so you can bound cleanup that way.
  3. What if cleanup throws? → The cleanup exception replaces or supplements the CE. If it's a non-CE exception, the coroutine fails with it, which turns a quiet cancellation into a crash path. Guard cleanup with its own try/catch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "use NonCancellable in finally". The senior answer explains that it swaps the Job, so it's only for withContext, explains why launch(NonCancellable) breaks structure, adds a timeout inside, and warns about cleanup exceptions turning cancellation into failure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An upload feature called api.abortUpload() in finally without NonCancellable. It never ran on cancel, and the backend accumulated about 200k orphaned multipart sessions per month until storage costs flagged it.

questions.promptHtml: TimeoutCancellationException extends CancellationException. What consequences does that have, and how do nested timeouts behave?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests whether the candidate can reason about timeouts as cancellation all the way through: propagation, catch blocks, nesting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since a TCE is a CE, it inherits cancellation semantics. Uncaught inside a launch, it ends that coroutine as cancelled, silently, without failing the parent or reaching a handler. Inside coroutineScope/runBlocking it propagates to the caller like any exception. With nesting, each timeout only handles its own TCE. withTimeoutOrNull returns null only if the TCE came from its timer. If an inner withTimeout fires, the inner TCE passes through the outer withTimeoutOrNull unchanged. And catching CancellationException to handle timeouts also swallows real cancellation, so I catch TimeoutCancellationException specifically.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Inside launch:
scope.launch {
    val data = withTimeout(3_000) { api.load() }   // times out
    render(data)                                   // never runs
}  // coroutine completes as "cancelled": no crash, no log, parent and siblings unaffected

That looks benign, but the user just sees nothing. If the timeout is a real failure for the UI, convert it to an error (catch TCE and return a failure/state).

  1. Nested timeouts: the kotlinx implementation of withTimeoutOrNull checks that the caught TCE's coroutine is its own timeout coroutine. Otherwise it rethrows:
val r = withTimeoutOrNull(10_000) {        // outer
    withTimeout(1_000) { slowCall() }      // inner fires at 1s -> TCE(inner)
}
// r is NOT null: the inner TCE propagates out of withTimeoutOrNull as an exception

So the effective deadline is the minimum of the nested timeouts, and the innermost fired timeout decides which exception you get.

  1. Telling timeout from cancellation:
try {
    withTimeout(2_000) { api.call() }
} catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) {
    // our timeout fired; caller still active -> safe to handle as an error
    showTimeoutError()
}
// A plain CancellationException from the caller being cancelled is NOT caught -> propagates correctly

Edge case: if the caller is cancelled at the same moment the timeout fires, you may still catch a TCE while the caller is cancelled. Call ensureActive() before doing user-visible work in the catch.

  1. Converting TCE to a real error at a layer boundary stops it from being silently treated as cancellation further up:
class NetworkTimeout(cause: Throwable) : IOException("timeout", cause)

suspend fun <T> withNetworkTimeout(ms: Long, block: suspend () -> T): T = try {
    withTimeout(ms) { block() }
} catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) {
    throw NetworkTimeout(e)          // now a failure: reaches error handling, retry policies, crash reporting
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (e: CancellationException) { showTimeout() } → shows "timeout" when the user simply left the screen.
  • Assuming the outer withTimeoutOrNull absorbs inner timeouts.
  • Putting withTimeout around a whole retry loop when you meant a per-attempt timeout, or the other way round. Be explicit about which budget each timeout guards.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does TCE trigger CoroutineExceptionHandler? → No. It's a CE.
  2. In async { withTimeout(..) {} }, what does await() throw? → The async completes as cancelled (with the TCE as cause), so await() throws a CE in the awaiting coroutine, which is the foreign CE problem (Q367). Convert it to a domain exception inside the async.
  3. Does withTimeout measure CPU time? → No, wall-clock time via the dispatcher's Delay (virtual time under runTest).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "it's thrown on timeout, you can catch it". The senior answer covers silent launch termination, the nested-timeout ownership check, the narrow catch, the race with outer cancellation, and converting it at a boundary into a real exception.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A repository caught CancellationException to map timeouts to "Server slow, retry?". Users who navigated back during a load got a retry dialog on the next screen. About 2% of sessions saw a phantom dialog.

questions.contextHtml:
A fitness app (1.2M DAU) shows a live leaderboard. The ViewModel polls every 10 s while the screen is visible. After the 5.4 release, backend RPS on /leaderboard rose from about 9k to 31k with no DAU change. Battery complaints went up and Android vitals shows "excessive wake-ups" on a subset of devices. Crashlytics non-fatals now show about 2M/day of:

Non-fatal: kotlinx.coroutines.JobCancellationException: Job was cancelled; job=SupervisorJobImpl{Cancelling}@4f1a2c
  at LeaderboardRepository.fetch(LeaderboardRepository.kt:41)

The 5.4 diff included a new safeApiCall helper, an OkHttp upgrade (4.11 → 4.12), and a refactor of the screen to a new Fragment.

suspend fun <T> safeApiCall(block: suspend () -> T): ApiResult<T> =
    runCatching { block() }
        .fold({ ApiResult.Ok(it) }, { crashlytics.recordException(it); ApiResult.Err(it) })

// ViewModel
init {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        while (true) {
            when (val r = safeApiCall { api.leaderboard() }) {
                is ApiResult.Ok -> _state.value = Ui.Data(r.value)
                is ApiResult.Err -> _state.value = Ui.Error(r.error)
            }
            pollDelay()
        }
    }
}
private suspend fun pollDelay() = runCatching { delay(10_000) }
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the investigation and the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back OkHttp" or "the new Fragment creates multiple ViewModels". These are plausible red herrings, but neither explains JobCancellationException being recorded 2M times or a loop that survives cancellation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the extra RPS from fewer clients polling more often, or more clients? Server logs by install ID tell me whether loops survive. Do the extra requests come from users who aren't on the screen? Session analytics joined with request timestamps. When did safeApiCall start being used? Is the poll in init, meaning it runs for the ViewModel's whole life and not just while visible?
  2. Immediate mitigation: A remote config flag that sets the poll interval to 60 s or disables polling, plus a server-side rate limit per install on /leaderboard. Then ship a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) runCatching around delay swallows cancellation. After viewModelScope is cancelled (onCleared), delay throws a CE immediately, runCatching eats it, and the loop goes round again. safeApiCall also eats the CE from the Retrofit call. The result is a hot loop that fires a request as fast as the cancelled call can fail and records a non-fatal each time. This matches both the RPS and the Crashlytics volume.
    • (b) The Fragment refactor scopes the ViewModel to the Activity, so polling continues off screen. That's plausible for "polls while not visible", but it wouldn't produce JobCancellationExceptions.
    • (c) OkHttp 4.12 retry behavior. Unlikely; nothing in the changelog matches, and it wouldn't produce CE logs.
  4. How I'd verify each: A local repro: open the screen, press back, watch Logcat/OkHttp logging. Requests keep firing with the ViewModel cleared. The coroutine debug agent / DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() shows the coroutine in the "Cancelling" state still running. For (b), log viewModelStoreOwner in onCreate. Server logs: requests from the same install at sub-second intervals confirm (a).
  5. Root cause: After onCleared() cancels viewModelScope, every cancellable suspension throws a CE immediately. Retrofit's suspend adapter still runs its suspendCancellableCoroutine block, which calls enqueue, and only then notices the cancelled Job and calls call.cancel(). Some of those requests get onto the wire before the cancel, so the server sees them. runCatching turns the CE into Err, which writes to _state (nobody collects it) and records a non-fatal. Then pollDelay() swallows the instant CE from delay and the loop goes round with no wait. Every ViewModel that has been cleared during the process lifetime becomes a busy loop that only stops when the process dies. Most iterations are cancelled before they're sent, which is why server RPS is 3.4x and not 1000x, while Crashlytics records every iteration (2M/day). I'd confirm the per-install request rate in server logs before quoting numbers.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: make safeApiCall cancellation-aware and delete the runCatching around delay.
    suspend fun <T> safeApiCall(block: suspend () -> T): ApiResult<T> =
    try {
        ApiResult.Ok(block())
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        if (e !is IOException) crashlytics.recordException(e)  // don't record expected network failures either
        ApiResult.Err(e)
    }
    • Long term: drive polling from the UI lifecycle (a flow { while (true) { emit(fetch()); delay(10_000) } } exposed via stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5_000)), see F5) so it stops when the screen isn't visible, not only when the ViewModel is cleared.
  7. Prevention: A lint/Detekt rule banning runCatching in suspend code. A unit test with runTest that cancels the ViewModel scope and asserts zero further API calls on a fake. A Crashlytics filter alert if any CE appears as a non-fatal.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't roll back OkHttp, which has no evidence and costs a release. I wouldn't add if (!isActive) break to the loop as the main fix, because it patches one symptom and leaves safeApiCall broken for 200 other call sites.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why didn't this crash or show in the UI? → _state updates after onCleared go nowhere. Nobody collects them anymore, so the bug is invisible except in metrics.
  • Would viewModelScope being a SupervisorJob matter? → No. Supervision affects child failure, not cancellation. The scope is cancelled in onCleared either way.
  • What if the server is non-idempotent? → For a GET, it's just load. For POSTs, swallowed cancellation can repeat writes, which needs idempotency keys (Q374).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "safe" wrapper with catch (Throwable) went into a shared networking module used by 14 features. Weeks later the backend team noticed traffic from users whose sessions had ended. Fixing one helper took 40% off mobile API traffic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames OkHttp/the Fragment without explaining the CE logs; doesn't know runCatching catches CE.
  • Hire: identifies swallowed cancellation in both safeApiCall and delay and fixes the helper.
  • Strong hire: explains the loop mechanics after cancel, verifies with server logs and DebugProbes, separates lifecycle-scoped polling (F5) as the long-term fix, and adds lint/tests/alerting.

questions.promptHtml: What is runInterruptible, how does it work, and when does it actually help?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real apps still call blocking Java APIs. The question tests whether you know how to bridge their interruption model to coroutine cancellation, and where that bridge doesn't reach.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: runInterruptible(context) { blockingCall() } runs a non-suspending block, by default on the current dispatcher or the context I pass (usually Dispatchers.IO). If the coroutine is cancelled while the block runs, it calls Thread.interrupt() on that thread. APIs that respond to interruption, like Thread.sleep, Object.wait, BlockingQueue.take, Future.get and NIO interruptible channels, then throw, and runInterruptible rethrows that as a CancellationException. It only helps with interruptible APIs. Classic socket InputStream.read and most JNI calls ignore interrupts, so for those I need the API's own cancel or close method.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism (simplified):

  1. Switch to the given context, as with withContext.
  2. Install a cancellation handler on the Job that interrupts the current thread, but only while the block is executing. A state machine guards this so the pooled thread isn't interrupted after the block has returned. Otherwise the next coroutine on that thread would get a spurious interrupt.
  3. Run the block. If it throws InterruptedException because of our interrupt, convert it to a CancellationException. Clear the interrupted flag before returning the thread to the pool.

What responds to Thread.interrupt():

Responds Doesn't respond
Thread.sleep, Object.wait, Thread.join java.io.InputStream.read on a socket/file (classic IO)
BlockingQueue.put/take, CountDownLatch.await, Future.get synchronized lock acquisition
NIO InterruptibleChannel ops (channel gets closed, ClosedByInterruptException) most JNI / native code
Lock.lockInterruptibly() CPU loops that never check Thread.interrupted()

The NIO case has a side effect: interrupting a thread blocked in FileChannel.read closes the channel. That's fine for cancellation, but surprising if the channel is shared.

OkHttp/Okio check the thread's interrupted state at some timeout and IO boundaries, so a synchronous call.execute() may abort with InterruptedIOException when interrupted. Don't build on that. Prefer the suspend API or call.cancel() (Q365).

Availability: runInterruptible is in kotlinx-coroutines-core (added in the 1.3.x line; available in all 1.6+ versions you'd use today).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Legacy SDK exposes a blocking Future
suspend fun loadModel(): Model = runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) {
    legacySdk.loadModelAsync().get()      // Future.get() -> InterruptedException on cancel -> CE
}

// Won't help: classic socket stream ignores interrupt
suspend fun readAll(socket: Socket): ByteArray = runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) {
    socket.getInputStream().readBytes()   // cancel does NOT unblock this
}
// Correct for sockets: close the resource on cancellation
suspend fun readAllCancellable(socket: Socket): ByteArray = coroutineScope {
    val finished = AtomicBoolean(false)
    val closer = launch {
        try { awaitCancellation() } finally { if (!finished.get()) socket.close() } // unblocks read
    }
    try {
        withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
            try {
                socket.getInputStream().readBytes()
            } catch (e: SocketException) {
                ensureActive()      // if we closed it because of cancellation, surface CE, not a failure
                throw e
            }
        }
    } finally {
        finished.set(true)          // normal completion: don't close the caller's socket
        closer.cancel()
    }
}

How the second correct example works: when the outer coroutine is cancelled, closer is cancelled too, and its finally closes the socket. The blocked read throws SocketException, and the ensureActive() turns that into a cancellation instead of a real failure. The finished flag stops the socket from being closed on the success path.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using runInterruptible around a suspend lambda. The block is non-suspending by signature, so you can't, but people then nest runBlocking inside it, which is a disaster.
  • Expecting it to stop native/JNI work.
  • Writing your own Thread.currentThread().interrupt() in invokeOnCancellation. That can interrupt whichever coroutine runs next on the pooled thread.
