sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just withContext(IO) { future.get() }? → Cancellation would be ignored until get() returns. The thread stays pinned and the coroutine stays Cancelling.
  2. Is the interrupted flag cleaned up? → Yes, runInterruptible handles clearing it so the pooled thread is reused cleanly.
  3. Alternative for CompletableFuture/ListenableFuture? → Use await() from the integration modules, which cancels the future (C10).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "it makes blocking code cancellable". The senior answer names exactly which APIs respond to interrupts, explains the pooled-thread safety problem, the NIO channel-closing side effect, and the close-the-resource alternative for sockets.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An on-device ML feature waited on Future.get() inside withContext(IO). Leaving the screen didn't free the thread. With 64 IO threads and an autoplay carousel, model loads eventually blocked all of IO until runInterruptible was introduced.

questions.promptHtml: When a coroutine running a Retrofit suspend call is cancelled, what happens to the HTTP request, on the client and on the server?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It connects coroutine cancellation to real networking. Seniors must know that "cancelled" on the client doesn't mean "didn't happen" on the server.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since Retrofit 2.6, suspend functions are implemented with suspendCancellableCoroutine around call.enqueue, plus invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() }. When the coroutine is cancelled, the continuation resumes immediately with a CE and OkHttp's call.cancel() runs. OkHttp then tears down the stream or connection, and its callback reports IOException("Canceled"), which is ignored because the continuation is already done. On the server, a cancel is just the client hanging up. If the request was already sent, the server may fully process it. So cancellation saves client resources and bandwidth, but it's not a rollback. Non-idempotent calls need idempotency keys.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timeline:

coroutine     ──suspend in await()────────X cancel()
                                          │ resume(CE) immediately; coroutine unwinds
OkHttp call   enqueue → connect → write request → [server processing] → read response
                                          │ call.cancel(): close socket / RST_STREAM (HTTP/2)
Server        receives full request?  YES → may complete the operation; response is discarded
              receives partial body?  usually aborts (depends on server framework)

Details that matter:

  • HTTP/2: cancel sends RST_STREAM for that stream only, and the shared connection survives. HTTP/1.1: the connection is closed and not returned to the pool, which costs a new TLS handshake for the next request.
  • Interceptors: an interceptor in the middle of chain.proceed() sees an IOException("Canceled"). Retry or auth interceptors that catch IOException and retry must check chain.call().isCanceled(), or they retry a call nobody wants.
  • Logging: you'll see java.io.IOException: Canceled in OkHttp logs or event listeners. It's expected noise for cancelled coroutines, not a network error. Filter it out of error metrics.
  • Blocking execute(): if you call call.execute() inside withContext(IO), coroutine cancellation does not cancel the call. Use the suspend API, or cancel explicitly: suspendCancellableCoroutine + enqueue, or invokeOnCancellation.
  • Response body streaming: for @Streaming downloads you get the ResponseBody once headers arrive. Cancellation after that point does nothing to the body unless you close it, so read inside use {} with cancellation checks per chunk.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Streaming download that honors cancellation and doesn't leak the connection
suspend fun download(url: String, dest: File) = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    api.download(url).use { body ->                    // @Streaming suspend fun download(@Url u: String): ResponseBody
        body.byteStream().use { input ->
            dest.outputStream().use { output ->
                val buf = ByteArray(64 * 1024)
                while (true) {
                    ensureActive()                     // check between 64 KB chunks
                    val n = input.read(buf)
                    if (n < 0) break
                    output.write(buf, 0, n)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming a cancelled POST didn't happen and letting the user resubmit, which causes duplicate orders (Q374).
  • Recording IOException: Canceled as a network failure, which inflates error rates in dashboards.
  • An auth interceptor retrying after Canceled.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Retrofit's Call<T> (non-suspend) cancel automatically? → No. Only the suspend adapter wires invokeOnCancellation. With Call.await() from Retrofit's KotlinExtensions you get the same wiring.
  2. What does OkHttp's EventListener report? → callFailed with IOException("Canceled"), or canceled() in OkHttp 4.x+ where the event exists. Verify against your OkHttp version.
  3. Can the server detect the cancel? → Only as a client disconnect. Most frameworks don't abort in-flight handlers, so treat it as "unknown outcome".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "Retrofit cancels the request". The senior answer explains the invokeOnCancellation mechanism, the HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2 cost, interceptor and logging implications, streaming bodies, and that server-side effects may still happen.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a "cancel previous search" change, a dashboard showed a 6x jump in "network errors". All of them were IOException: Canceled from intentional cancellations, and the alert was paging on-call for nothing.

questions.promptHtml: The kotlinx.coroutines docs describe a resource leak with withTimeout even when the code "looks" correct. Explain the race and the fix.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It separates people who've read the docs and understood asynchronous cancellation from people who know the API names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The timeout fires asynchronously relative to the block. The block can finish and produce a value, say a freshly opened resource, and the timeout can still fire before control returns to the caller. withTimeout then throws a TCE and the value is discarded, so the resource you returned is never closed. The documented fix is to never let a resource be owned only by the return value. Store it in a variable declared outside the timeout block, assigned the moment it's acquired, and close it in a finally outside the timeout.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
// LEAKS occasionally
val resource = withTimeout(60) {
    delay(50)
    Resource()          // acquired
}                       // <- timeout fires around here: Resource() returned but TCE thrown instead
resource.close()        // never reached

Why it's possible:

  1. withTimeout schedules a cancellation of the block at T = 60 ms on the dispatcher's Delay.
  2. The block resumes from delay(50) at about 50 ms plus scheduling jitter. On a busy dispatcher it may run at 59 ms. It constructs Resource().
  3. Between the block returning and withTimeout handing the value back, the timer fires and the coroutine is cancelled. Because of the prompt cancellation guarantee on resumption (Q368), the caller gets a TCE instead of the value. The value is lost.

The docs demonstrate this by running 10k coroutines on a pool, each acquiring a counted resource, and showing that the "acquired" counter usually doesn't return to zero.

The documented fix:

var resource: Resource? = null
try {
    withTimeout(60) {
        delay(50)
        resource = Resource()     // ownership recorded the instant it exists
    }
    // use resource
} finally {
    resource?.close()             // runs on success, timeout, or outer cancellation
}

This generalizes. A value that requires cleanup must never exist only as the in-flight return value of a cancellable operation. That includes withContext returns (the same prompt-cancellation loss) and async results that are never awaited.

Android-relevant resources where this bites: Cursor, ParcelFileDescriptor, MediaPlayer/MediaCodec, BluetoothGatt connections, camera devices, WakeLock, OkHttp Response (not closed → connection leak, plus the OkHttp "A connection to ... was leaked" warning).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Generic helper: acquire under timeout without leaking
suspend fun <R : AutoCloseable> acquireWithTimeout(ms: Long, acquire: suspend () -> R): R {
    var acquired: R? = null
    try {
        withTimeout(ms) { acquired = acquire() }
        return acquired!!
    } catch (t: Throwable) {
        acquired?.close()          // timed out (or failed) after acquiring -> release
        throw t
    }
}

Caveat: if acquire() itself is interrupted halfway, for example a socket half-open inside a library, only the library can clean that up. The helper covers the "acquired but lost" window, not partial acquisition.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing try { withTimeout { r = open(); r.use { ... } } } is enough. It is if all use happens inside the block. The leak only happens when the resource escapes through the return value.
  • Thinking this is a timeout-only problem. Any cancellation at the resumption boundary of withContext has the same loss.
  • Fixing it by switching to withTimeoutOrNull and returning the resource. Same race, the value is just lost as null instead of as an exception.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you detect this in production? → Leak counters: a reference-counted wrapper with StrictMode.detectLeakedClosableObjects() in debug, OkHttp's connection-leak log, LeakCanary for objects holding native handles.
  2. Does NonCancellable help? → Wrapping the acquisition in NonCancellable defeats the timeout. Don't. Use the outer-variable pattern.
  3. Why doesn't the library just return the value if the block completed? → The prompt cancellation guarantee is deliberate. It stops code from continuing in a cancelled context, such as updating the UI of a destroyed screen. Losing values is the documented price.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer explains timeouts but misses the race. The senior answer explains the asynchronous fire between block completion and return, links it to the prompt cancellation guarantee, gives the outer-variable fix, and generalizes to withContext, async and Android native resources.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A BLE feature acquired a BluetoothGatt inside withTimeout(10_000) { connect() } and returned it. On flaky connections, timeouts at about 10 s leaked GATT clients until the stack hit its client limit and every new connect failed with status 133, until a phone reboot.

questions.promptHtml: What happens if a coroutine that is not cancelled receives a CancellationException, for example from await() on a cancelled Deferred? Why is that dangerous?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a subtle, real bug class: coroutines dying silently. Only people who have debugged it tend to know it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The coroutine machinery can't tell "I was cancelled" from "some code threw a CE at me". If a CE escapes the body of an active launch, that coroutine completes as cancelled. Its parent isn't notified of a failure, no handler runs, and nothing is logged, so the work just stops. A common source is await() on a Deferred that was cancelled, for instance one cached in a shared map and cancelled by another caller's scope. The defense is to treat a CE as cancellation only when ensureActive() confirms my Job is cancelled. Otherwise convert it into a real error.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Sources of foreign CEs:

  1. deferred.await() where the deferred was cancelled. await throws a CE (the deferred's cancellation exception) into a caller that is still active.
  2. A Job/Deferred shared across scopes, such as an in-memory "single-flight" cache of Deferred<Token> created in screen A's scope. Screen A closes, the deferred is cancelled, and screen B's await() gets a CE.
  3. withTimeout TCEs escaping their scope, for instance a TCE thrown out of an async and seen at await().
  4. Java/library code throwing java.util.concurrent.CancellationException, for example Future.get() on a cancelled FutureTask. On the JVM, it's the same class.
  5. Your own code throwing CE as a "stop" signal.
Screen B coroutine (active) ──await()──► cachedDeferred (cancelled by Screen A's scope)
         ◄── throws CancellationException
B's launch body exits with CE ──► B's Job: Cancelled (silently). Parent: unaffected. No log.
UI: spinner forever.

Why the library behaves this way: completion with a CE is defined as "cancelled", by type and not by origin. There's a long-standing kotlinx.coroutines discussion about the ambiguity. There's no built-in fix in 1.10, so you handle it at the boundary.

Defense pattern:

suspend fun <T> Deferred<T>.awaitOrFail(): T = try {
    await()
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()           // if WE are cancelled, rethrow as cancellation
    throw IllegalStateException("Upstream work was cancelled", e)  // otherwise: real failure, visible
}

Design fixes that remove the source:

  • Shared single-flight work belongs in a scope that outlives its callers, like an app-scoped CoroutineScope (C7). Then a caller leaving doesn't cancel the shared job. Use per-caller await() only.
  • Don't use job.cancel() to signal "this request is obsolete" to other awaiters. Complete a CompletableDeferred exceptionally with a domain exception instead.
  • Don't throw CE for control flow. Return, or throw a domain exception.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BUG: token refresh deferred lives in the first caller's scope
class TokenCache(private val api: AuthApi) {
    private var inFlight: Deferred<String>? = null
    suspend fun token(): String = coroutineScope {
        val d = inFlight ?: async { api.refresh() }.also { inFlight = it }   // child of caller #1
        d.await()   // caller #2 gets CE if caller #1's screen closed mid-refresh
    }
}

// FIX: shared work in an owning scope; callers only await
class TokenCacheFixed(private val api: AuthApi, private val appScope: CoroutineScope) {
    private val lock = Mutex()
    private var inFlight: Deferred<String>? = null
    suspend fun token(): String {
        val d = lock.withLock {
            inFlight?.takeIf { it.isActive } ?: appScope.async { api.refresh() }.also { inFlight = it }
        }
        return d.await()
    }
}

(The full token-refresh race design is owned by C8/X. Here the point is who owns the Deferred.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } everywhere. That's correct for your own cancellation, but it also silently propagates foreign CEs.
  • Blaming "the coroutine just stopped" on the dispatcher or lifecycle.
  • Mixing Future-based Java libraries and assuming their CE means coroutine cancellation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does awaitAll have the same issue? → Yes. If any deferred is cancelled, awaitAll throws a CE in the caller.
  2. How would you debug a silently stopped coroutine? → invokeOnCompletion { cause -> log(cause) } on the job, DebugProbes, and logging in a catch (e: CancellationException) that checks coroutineContext.isActive. If you're active, it's foreign.
  3. Can this happen with withContext? → Only if the block throws a CE it got from elsewhere. Then withContext rethrows it and the caller treats it as cancellation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "await throws if the deferred is cancelled". The senior answer explains completion classification by type, lists the real sources, gives the ensureActive()-based conversion, and fixes the ownership design so shared work lives in an owning scope.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared image-prefetch cache stored Deferred<Bitmap> created in RecyclerView item scopes. When items scrolled away, their deferreds were cancelled, and other cells awaiting the same URL silently stopped loading, leaving about 3% of grid cells blank with zero errors logged.

questions.promptHtml: What is the "prompt cancellation guarantee" in kotlinx.coroutines, and what does it imply for code like withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { db.insert(x) }?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows deep runtime knowledge: work can complete while the caller still observes cancellation, which matters for correctness of writes and UI.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Since kotlinx.coroutines 1.4, withContext and suspendCancellableCoroutine guarantee that if the Job is cancelled while the coroutine is suspended, it won't resume normally, even when the result has already arrived and is waiting to be dispatched back. For withContext(IO) { db.insert(x) }, that means the insert can commit on IO, then the caller is cancelled before Main runs the continuation, and the caller gets a CancellationException instead of the inserted ID. So "my suspend call threw CE" does not mean "it didn't happen". Writes must be idempotent or confirmed separately.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Main:   launch { val id = withContext(IO) { db.insert(x) }; show(id) }
IO:                        insert() commits ── result ready ─► dispatch continuation to Main
Main:                         [user presses back → scope.cancel()]
Main:   continuation runs: Job is cancelled → throw CE instead of returning id
        show(id) never runs; the row EXISTS in the DB

Before 1.4, a continuation could resume normally after cancellation if the result arrived first. That's the "atomic" resumption behavior: code then ran in a cancelled context, for example touching views of a destroyed Fragment. The library changed it to prompt cancellation, and the docs document the trade-off: returned values can be lost when the caller is cancelled. The exception is the withContext(NonCancellable) pattern when no dispatch is needed on exit.

Consequences:

  1. Lost return values. Anything that needs cleanup and is returned across a cancellable boundary can leak (Q366). For callbacks, CancellableContinuation.resume(value) { cause, value, ctx -> close(value) } gives you a hook when the value is rejected. The three-parameter onCancellation form is in current releases (1.9+/1.10); older code uses the single-cause overload.
  2. Unknown outcome of writes. A cancelled saveOrder() may have committed. Design for it: idempotency keys, upserts, or re-reading state on the next screen.
  3. UI safety (the reason it exists). After a cancelled withContext, code never runs in a destroyed screen, so show(id) can't touch dead views.

Dispatchers.Main.immediate nuance: if the result comes back on the same thread and no dispatch is needed, there's no window, but you can't count on that in general.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Treat the write as "maybe done" on cancellation
fun submit(order: Order) {
    val key = order.idempotencyKey            // generated once per user intent
    viewModelScope.launch {
        try {
            val id = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { repo.saveOrder(order, key) }
            _state.value = Saved(id)
        } catch (e: CancellationException) {
            // Do not assume "not saved". Next screen re-reads by key; server dedupes by key.
            throw e
        }
    }
}

// Callback bridge that doesn't leak a value rejected by prompt cancellation
suspend fun openDevice(manager: DeviceManager): Device = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    manager.open { device ->
        cont.resume(device) { _, rejected, _ -> rejected.close() }   // called iff value was not delivered
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping withContext in NonCancellable to "make sure we get the result". That defeats lifecycle cancellation.
  • Telling users "save failed" on CE. It might have succeeded.
  • Assuming the guarantee covers plain suspendCoroutine. It doesn't, because that primitive isn't cancellable at all.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Deferred.await() have the same behavior? → Yes. If the awaiting coroutine is cancelled while the deferred completes, await throws CE in the waiter.
  2. Is the work inside withContext cancelled too? → Yes, the block's Job is a child. But a block that already returned can't be undone, and the commit stands.
  3. How to unit-test this window? → With StandardTestDispatcher: run the IO part, cancel the scope before runCurrent() on the Main scheduler, then assert the side effect happened and the continuation didn't run.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer doesn't know the term. The senior answer explains the dispatch window, the 1.4 change and why it was made (UI safety), and the consequences: lost values (the resume onCancellation hook) and unknown write outcomes (idempotency).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A notes app showed "Couldn't save, try again" whenever the save coroutine was cancelled by a back press. Users retried and created duplicate notes. The first save had already committed in about 98% of those cases.

questions.promptHtml: What happens if a coroutine is cancelled while it's inside a Room withTransaction { } block, or during a suspend DAO call? Is partial data written?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Data integrity under cancellation is a senior concern. Candidates need to reason about transaction boundaries rather than guess.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Room's withTransaction follows "commit only if the block completes normally". If the coroutine is cancelled at a suspension point inside the block, the CE propagates out, the transaction is ended without being marked successful, and SQLite rolls back. So you don't get half of the block's writes. Two caveats. First, if cancellation arrives after the commit, the caller may still see a CE (prompt cancellation), so the data is saved but the caller thinks it failed. Second, a long-running SQL statement is only interrupted where Room can cancel it. Cancellability of an individual query has varied by Room version, so I'd treat a single statement as running to completion.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
How withTransaction works (Room 2.x, room-ktx):

  1. It acquires a dedicated transaction thread from Room's transaction executor and runs the block in a coroutine context bound to that thread. DAO suspend calls inside the block reuse the same connection.
  2. It calls beginTransaction(), runs the block, calls setTransactionSuccessful() only if the block returns normally, then endTransaction() in a finally.
  3. A thrown CE from any suspension inside the block skips setTransactionSuccessful(), so endTransaction() rolls back.
withTransaction {
   dao.insertOrder(o)      // written inside txn (not yet visible to other connections)
   dao.insertItems(items)  // ← cancelled here → CE
   dao.updateStock(...)    // never runs
}                          // endTransaction() without success → ROLLBACK: order + items gone

Cases to reason about:

Situation Data outcome Caller sees
Cancelled at a suspension inside the block rolled back CE
Cancelled while a single SQL statement is executing statement usually finishes, then the next suspension throws → rolled back CE
Cancelled after the block returns, during commit/dispatch back committed CE (prompt cancellation)
Non-suspend @Transaction DAO method called from withContext(IO) runs to completion (blocking, not cancellable) CE after it returns
Non-Room suspend work inside the block (network!) holds the write lock for its whole duration; if cancelled → rollback CE

Version notes, hedged:

  • Recent Room 2.x generated code for suspend @Query functions passes a CancellationSignal (visible in CoroutinesRoom.execute overloads in room-ktx API dumps) so a cancelled coroutine can abort a long SELECT. Treat this as best effort and verify against your Room version's generated code.
  • Room 2.7+ (KMP) adds the useWriterConnection { it.immediateTransaction { } } connection APIs. The same commit-or-rollback principle applies. Check the current docs for exact cancellation behavior.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun placeOrder(o: Order, items: List<Item>) {
    // Do network BEFORE the transaction; keep the txn short and DB-only
    val priced = api.price(items)
    db.withTransaction {
        dao.insertOrder(o)
        dao.insertItems(priced)
        dao.decrementStock(priced)
    }  // all-or-nothing even under cancellation
}

// Work that must not be abandoned when the screen leaves: run it in an owning scope
class OrderRepository(private val db: AppDatabase, private val appScope: CoroutineScope) {
    suspend fun placeOrderDurable(o: Order, items: List<Item>) =
        appScope.async { placeOrder(o, items) }.await()   // screen cancel stops awaiting, not the write
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Network calls inside withTransaction: they hold the write lock for seconds, and cancellation then rolls back everything, including writes the user expected.
  • Calling runBlocking inside a transaction block, or switching dispatchers to something unrelated inside it. The Room docs warn that the block must keep its transaction context, and other threads can't see the transaction.
  • Assuming "CE from save = nothing written" (see the commit-then-cancel row).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a launch inside withTransaction write within the transaction? → It's a child with the transaction context, but writes after the block has returned are outside the transaction or fail. Don't spawn concurrent work inside a transaction.
  2. Is a Flow-returning DAO query cancelled when the collector stops? → Yes. The observer/invalidation tracker registration is removed when collection is cancelled.
  3. How do you guarantee the write happens even if the user leaves? → Use an app-scoped coroutine or WorkManager (C7) for durable writes. The transaction gives atomicity, not durability against cancellation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "Room handles it" or "it might write partial data". The senior answer explains commit-on-normal-completion, so CE means rollback, plus the commit-then-CE window, non-cancellable running statements, keeping network out of transactions, and owning-scope durability. Version-specific details are hedged.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout flow called the pricing API inside withTransaction. On slow networks users backed out, the transaction rolled back the cart snapshot, and support tickets reported "my cart disappeared". Moving the network call outside the transaction fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: How does cancellation propagate between parent and child? And what happens if I launch into a scope that has already been cancelled?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Silent no-op launches into dead scopes are a common "button does nothing" bug. The propagation direction tests the basic mental model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cancellation flows down. Cancelling a Job cancels all its children recursively, and the parent then waits in the Cancelling state until they finish. Cancelling a child, or a child completing with a CE, does not cancel the parent or its siblings. Only a real failure, a non-CE exception, propagates up (C6). If you launch into a scope whose Job is already cancelled, launch still returns a Job, but that Job is born cancelled. With default start, the body never runs: no code, no finally, no error. It silently does nothing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Parent (cancel())
           /       |        \
      child A   child B   child C        ← all receive cancel, unwind via CE
      parent stays "Cancelling" until A, B, C complete → then "Cancelled"

             Parent (active)
           /       |        \
      child A   child B(cancel())  child C   ← only B cancelled; parent & A, C unaffected

Launching into a cancelled scope:

  • scope.launch {} creates a child of a cancelled Job. Attaching it immediately cancels the child.
  • With CoroutineStart.DEFAULT, a coroutine cancelled before it is dispatched completes as cancelled without executing its body.
  • With CoroutineStart.ATOMIC (experimental) or UNDISPATCHED, the body starts and is cancelled at its first suspension. Builders are covered in C2.
  • Typical Android triggers: a custom CoroutineScope(Job()) field in a singleton that got cancel()ed once (on logout, in a release() method) and is reused afterwards, or a scope cancelled in onDestroyView but held by an adapter that outlives the view.

Cancel with a cause: job.cancel("logout") or job.cancel(CancellationException("logout", cause)) makes the reason visible to ensureActive() callers and invokeOnCompletion, which helps a lot when debugging.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SessionManager {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default)

    fun logout() = scope.cancel("logout")      // BUG if the manager is reused after logout

    fun refreshProfile() = scope.launch {      // after logout(): returns a cancelled Job, body never runs
        repo.refresh()
    }
}

// Fix: cancel children, keep the scope reusable (or recreate the scope deliberately)
class SessionManagerFixed {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default)
    fun logout() = scope.coroutineContext.cancelChildren(CancellationException("logout"))
    fun refreshProfile() = scope.launch { repo.refresh() }
}

(cancel vs cancelChildren as API design belongs to C4. Here the point is that a dead scope silently drops work.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting an exception when launching into a dead scope. There isn't one. Assert scope.isActive in debug builds if this matters.
  • Putting critical cleanup in the finally of a coroutine that might never start.
  • Believing a cancelled child cancels the parent "because it's structured".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I detect the dead-scope case? → Check the returned job.isCancelled right after launch in debug builds, or add require(scope.isActive).
  2. Does async into a cancelled scope behave the same? → Yes. Its await() then throws a CE in the caller (Q367).
  3. Does a child cancelled with a custom CancellationException subclass propagate to the parent? → No. Any CE subclass is treated as cancellation and stays local.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "cancelling the parent cancels children". The senior answer adds: the parent waits for children, a child's cancellation doesn't go up, launches into dead scopes are silent no-ops with no finally, cancel causes help debugging, and it shows the reusable-singleton bug.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a logout/login cycle in a single process, "pull to refresh" did nothing until the app was restarted. The singleton's scope had been cancel()ed on logout, and every later launch was a no-op.

questions.contextHtml:
A video app tracks playback_session_end with watch time, which product uses for content payouts. Analytics shows about 4% of sessions have a start event but no end, and on Android only (iOS is 0.3%). It's worst when users swipe the player Fragment away (12%) and nearly 0% when the video plays to the end. Engineers suspect the analytics SDK batching (it flushes every 30 s) and Doze on Samsung devices.

// PlayerViewModel
fun startSession(videoId: String) {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        val start = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime()
        analytics.track("playback_session_start", videoId)     // suspend fun
        try {
            player.awaitCompletion()                           // suspends until playback ends
        } finally {
            val watched = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() - start
            analytics.track("playback_session_end", videoId, watched)   // suspend fun -> writes to Room queue
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain the metrics, and fix it so the event is reliably recorded.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Flush the analytics SDK on onStop" or "it's Doze". It doesn't explain why completion-to-end is fine and swipe-away is broken, or why the finally "doesn't run".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is analytics.track a suspend function that enqueues to Room? (If yes, it's a cancellable suspension.) Does swipe-away clear the ViewModel? (onCleared cancels viewModelScope.) Do we have Room queue rows for the missing events? That tells me "never enqueued" from "enqueued but not uploaded".
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an outage, but payouts depend on it. A quick hotfix plus backfilling estimates of missing sessions server-side from heartbeat events, if we have them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The finally runs in a cancelled coroutine. analytics.track suspends (Room withContext), throws a CE immediately, and the event is never enqueued. This matches swipe-away (cancellation) vs natural completion (no cancellation).
    • (b) SDK batching loses queued events on process death. It's possible, but events are persisted in Room, and the rows would exist. Easy to rule out.
    • (c) Doze/OEM killing. That would affect completion too, so it doesn't match the pattern.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test with runTest: start a session, cancel the scope, and assert the fake analytics received end. It fails. Debug logging in finally shows it's entered but track throws JobCancellationException. A Room DB inspection (App Inspection) shows no queued end rows for swiped sessions, which rules out (b).
  5. Root cause: On cancellation, awaitCompletion() throws a CE, so finally runs. But the coroutine's Job is cancelled, so analytics.track(...), which suspends through Room's withContext, throws a CE on entry. The event is never written.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: wrap the suspending cleanup in NonCancellable, bounded by a timeout.
    } finally {
    val watched = SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() - start
    withContext(NonCancellable) {
        withTimeoutOrNull(1_000) { analytics.track("playback_session_end", videoId, watched) }
    }
}
    • Long term: make track() non-suspending. It should append synchronously to an in-memory queue that an app-scoped writer drains to Room. Analytics must never depend on the caller's lifecycle. Add a periodic heartbeat (every 30 s) so a process kill loses at most 30 s of watch time.
  7. Prevention: A review checklist item: "suspend calls in finally need NonCancellable". A test template for "cleanup on cancel". An analytics data-quality alert on the start/end ratio per platform, which catches regressions in a day instead of at payout reconciliation.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't make the whole session NonCancellable or launch it in GlobalScope. That keeps the player coroutine alive past the screen. I wouldn't rely on onStop flushes, which don't fix the cancelled enqueue.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Process death on swipe? → finally never runs on a kill. That's why the heartbeat or a durable start record (reconciled server-side) is the real guarantee.
  • Would lifecycleScope instead of viewModelScope change anything? → It would cancel even earlier (on DESTROYED, including config changes). It's the same bug, and more frequent.
  • Why is iOS at 0.3%? → A different concurrency model (likely a synchronous enqueue). The platform delta is a strong signal that the bug is client logic, not backend.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A podcast app's "resume position" was saved in finally via a suspend DAO and silently failed on every back press. Users restarted episodes from 0 and nobody connected it to cancellation for months. The fix was 3 lines of NonCancellable plus a heartbeat save.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Doze/SDK theories; doesn't know suspend calls in finally throw after cancel.
  • Hire: identifies the cancelled finally and applies withContext(NonCancellable).
  • Strong hire: also bounds it with a timeout, decouples analytics from caller lifecycle, handles process death with heartbeats, adds a ratio alert and a cancellation test.

questions.contextHtml:
A banking app's home screen calls a third-party fraud-check SDK before showing balances. The SDK only exposes a blocking riskScore(): Int. The team wrapped it in a 2 s timeout so a slow SDK can't block the screen:

suspend fun riskScoreOrDefault(): Int =
    withTimeoutOrNull(2_000) {
        withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { fraudSdk.riskScore() }   // blocking, sometimes 8–15 s on poor networks
    } ?: DEFAULT_SCORE

Field metrics: home-screen p50 is 900 ms, but p95 is 9.4 s and p99 is 15.2 s. That's the SDK's latency, not 2 s. 1.8M DAU, 40% on 3G/poor networks in some regions. Product insists on "never wait more than 2 s". A teammate says the IO dispatcher is saturated because a Perfetto trace shows 40+ IO threads busy.
questions.promptHtml: Why doesn't the timeout work, and how do you actually enforce the 2 s budget?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase IO parallelism" or "use withTimeout instead of OrNull". Neither changes the fact that blocking code can't be cancelled.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the SDK have an async/callback API, a cancel method, or a timeout config? Is the call thread-safe and allowed to run concurrently (could we start it earlier)? Is DEFAULT_SCORE acceptable to the risk team, or must we block the transaction later instead? Do the IO threads in the trace belong to this SDK?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop waiting for the result after 2 s, even though the SDK call itself can't be stopped. Detach the waiting from the blocking work (below), and ship that behind a flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The timeout fires at 2 s, but withContext(IO) can't return until the blocking riskScore() returns. The timeout cancels the child, the child stays in Cancelling while the IO thread is blocked, and withTimeoutOrNull must wait for its child to complete (structured concurrency) before returning null. So the caller waits for the full SDK latency. Most likely.
    • (b) IO saturation. The 40+ threads are mostly SDK calls stuck for up to 15 s. That's a consequence of (a) piling up across refreshes (pull-to-refresh, re-entry), not the cause.
    • (c) Main thread contention. Unlikely, p50 is fine.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test with a fake SDK that does Thread.sleep(10_000): withTimeoutOrNull returns after about 10 s, not 2 s, which reproduces it. A Perfetto trace shows the IO worker in riskScore for 9 s after the timeout fired. DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() shows the child "Cancelling" with an IO thread in a native/socket read. Counting IO workers inside SDK frames confirms (b) is downstream.
  5. Root cause: A timeout is cancellation, and cancellation is cooperative. Blocking code has no cancellation points, and structured concurrency makes the parent wait for its child, so the timeout can't return early. Adding runInterruptible helps only if the SDK's blocking path responds to Thread.interrupt(). Socket reads in classic java.io typically don't.
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: run the blocking work outside the caller's structure, in an app-owned scope, and time out only the waiting.
    class RiskRepository(private val appScope: CoroutineScope, private val io: CoroutineDispatcher) {
    // Bounded concurrency so stuck SDK calls can't eat the IO pool
    private val sdkDispatcher = io.limitedParallelism(2)

    suspend fun riskScoreOrDefault(): Int {
        val work = appScope.async(sdkDispatcher) { fraudSdk.riskScore() }  // not a child of the caller
        return withTimeoutOrNull(2_000) { work.await() } ?: DEFAULT_SCORE   // await IS cancellable
    }
}
    The blocked thread keeps running until the SDK returns, but the screen gets its answer at 2 s. limitedParallelism(2) caps the damage at 2 threads. I'd also cache the in-flight Deferred so repeated refreshes reuse one call instead of stacking more.
    • Also try runInterruptible(sdkDispatcher) { fraudSdk.riskScore() } inside that async. If the SDK uses interruptible waits, threads come back sooner. Measure it, don't assume.
    • Long term: ask the vendor for an async API with cancellation or a configurable timeout, and start the risk check earlier (at app start or login) so the home screen rarely waits at all.
  7. Prevention: Lint/inspection for blocking calls wrapped in withTimeout without runInterruptible or detachment. A latency SLO alert on home p95. A fake-SDK test asserting the 2 s budget is honored.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Detaching breaks structured concurrency on purpose. The work outlives the caller, so it needs an owning scope, bounded parallelism and dedup, or it becomes a leak. I wouldn't raise IO parallelism, which only lets more threads get stuck. I wouldn't use GlobalScope (no ownership, no testability). And I wouldn't kill threads.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Risk team says a default score is unacceptable? → Then the budget conflicts with the requirement. Show balances with the score pending and gate transactions on it, rather than blocking the home render.
  • What if riskScore() isn't thread-safe? → limitedParallelism(1) plus single-flight dedup.
  • Does withTimeout behave differently? → Same blocking wait, but it throws a TCE afterwards. Still about 9 s.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A KYC flow wrapped a blocking OCR SDK in withTimeout(3_000) and dashboards showed "timeouts" taking 20 s. Detaching the work into an owned scope with a 1-thread dispatcher hit the 3 s budget and also stopped the SDK from occupying 30 IO threads during retries.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: thinks the timeout should have worked; suggests more threads.
  • Hire: explains cooperative cancellation and that the parent waits for a blocked child; suggests runInterruptible with caveats.
  • Strong hire: separates "stop waiting" from "stop working", detaches into an owned scope with bounded parallelism and dedup, identifies IO saturation as a downstream symptom, and pushes the product conversation about defaults.

questions.contextHtml:
Post-incident review. A QR-scanner feature opens Camera2 through a callback wrapper under a 3 s timeout. Over two weeks, the "camera unavailable" rate rose from 0.2% to 3.1% of scanner opens. It's concentrated on low-end devices and recovers only after the app process restarts. Logcat from an affected device:

E CameraService: Camera "0" is already open by client com.example.app (pid 8812)
W CameraDevice-JV-0: ... ERROR_CAMERA_IN_USE

The code (unchanged for months), plus a change two weeks ago that cut the timeout from 5 s to 3 s:

suspend fun openCamera(id: String): CameraDevice = withTimeout(3_000) {
    suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
        manager.openCamera(id, object : CameraDevice.StateCallback() {
            override fun onOpened(device: CameraDevice) { cont.resume(device) }
            override fun onDisconnected(device: CameraDevice) { device.close() }
            override fun onError(device: CameraDevice, error: Int) {
                device.close()
                if (cont.isActive) cont.resumeWithException(CameraOpenException(error))
            }
        }, handler)
    }
}
// caller
val device = openCamera("0")
try { startPreview(device) } finally { device.close() }

Red herrings in the timeline: a CameraX version bump in an unrelated feature, and an Android 14 security patch rollout on two OEMs.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the review: root cause, why it got worse two weeks ago, the fix, and the action items.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Close the camera in onPause" or "revert the timeout to 5 s". Reverting hides the bug by making the race rarer. onPause doesn't help because the leaked CameraDevice reference was never returned to anyone.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What's the p95 camera open time on low-end devices? (If it's close to 3 s, the timeout races onOpened.) Is the rise aligned with the timeout change rollout percentage? Do affected sessions show a scanner timeout before the "in use" error?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise the timeout back to 5 s via remote config. That reduces frequency, but I'd be explicit that it isn't the fix. Add a process-level guard that closes any tracked open device when the scanner screen is destroyed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) A cancellation race leaks the opened device. The timeout fires (or the user leaves) while the open is in flight. Later, onOpened(device) arrives and calls cont.resume(device) on a cancelled continuation. The value is silently dropped and nobody ever closes that CameraDevice. The camera stays held by our process until it dies. Shortening 5 → 3 s pushed more opens past the deadline on slow devices, roughly from 0.5% to 4% of opens if their p95 sits near 3 s.
    • (b) The timeout fired just after onOpened resumed but before the caller got the value (prompt cancellation, Q366/Q368). Same leak, smaller window.
    • (c) CameraX bump or the OEM patch. They don't explain "recovers only after process restart" or the correlation with the timeout change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics breadcrumbs: a scanner timeout followed by "camera in use" in the same session. A reproduction with a fake slow CameraManager delaying onOpened by 3.5 s, then asserting device.close() was called (it isn't). adb shell dumpsys media.camera shows our pid still holding camera 0 after leaving the scanner. Rollout cohort analysis: a 3 s vs 5 s cohort comparison of the error rate.
  5. Root cause: suspendCancellableCoroutine has no handling for a value that arrives after cancellation. cont.resume(device) on a cancelled continuation is ignored and the CameraDevice is orphaned. There's no invokeOnCancellation either, so nothing tracks a pending open that completes after we stopped waiting. The value is also lost if cancellation happens between resume and dispatch (prompt cancellation).
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: close rejected values and late arrivals.
    suspend fun openCamera(id: String): CameraDevice = withTimeout(3_000) {
    suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
        manager.openCamera(id, object : CameraDevice.StateCallback() {
            override fun onOpened(device: CameraDevice) {
                // onCancellation runs iff the value was not delivered (cancelled before or during dispatch)
                cont.resume(device) { _, rejected, _ -> rejected.close() }
            }
            override fun onDisconnected(device: CameraDevice) { device.close() }
            override fun onError(device: CameraDevice, error: Int) {
                device.close()
                if (cont.isActive) cont.resumeWithException(CameraOpenException(error))
            }
        }, handler)
    }
}
    With the resume(value, onCancellation) overload, both windows are covered: an onOpened that arrives after cancellation, and a value rejected because the caller was cancelled before dispatch. (The three-parameter lambda is in current kotlinx.coroutines releases. On older versions use the single-cause overload and close the captured device.)
    • Long term: one camera-owner component, lifecycle-bound, that tracks the open device and closes it on screen destroy regardless of how open/close coroutines interleave. Or move to CameraX, which manages this lifecycle.
  7. Prevention: A rule for every callback bridge that yields a closeable: use resume(value) { close } and pair it with invokeOnCancellation (C10 covers the bridging patterns). A test harness with fake slow callbacks around the timeout boundary. A Crashlytics metric for "camera in use by own pid". And any timeout-tuning change needs a check of p95 latency against the new deadline.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't remove the timeout, since users would stare at a black screen. I wouldn't use NonCancellable for the open, which defeats leaving the screen. I wouldn't blame the OEM patch without evidence. Reverting to 5 s is only mitigation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does cancellableContinuation.isActive checking in onOpened fix it? → Only partly. You'd close it when !isActive, but the prompt-cancellation window after a successful resume still leaks. The onCancellation overload covers both.
  • What if the caller's try/finally is reached? → Then the caller owns the device and closes it. The leak is strictly the "never delivered" path.
  • Why does a process restart fix it? → The camera service releases devices held by a dead client. The leak is per process.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A barcode feature leaked MediaCodec instances the same way. A late onOutputFormatChanged resumed cancelled continuations. Decoder limits (often 16 or fewer instances on low-end chips) were exhausted after about 20 quick open/close cycles. Closing rejected values fixed it in a 6-line diff.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames OEM/CameraX; revert-the-timeout is the whole answer.
  • Hire: identifies the late onOpened resuming a cancelled continuation and adds a close-on-cancel path.
  • Strong hire: also covers the prompt-cancellation window with resume(value, onCancellation), ties the regression to the 5 → 3 s change with cohort data, and proposes an owner component, tests at the timeout boundary and a review rule.

questions.promptHtml: A user cancels a coroutine that is mid-way through a non-idempotent operation, such as submitting an order. What guarantees does cancellation give you about the side effect, and how do you design for it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cancellation is a client-side event. Seniors must separate "my coroutine stopped" from "the operation did not happen", and design for the gap.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cancellation guarantees only that my coroutine stops waiting and unwinds. It guarantees nothing about the side effect. The HTTP request may be fully processed by the server, a Room write may have committed just before the CE (prompt cancellation), and a half-sent upload may or may not have been applied. So non-idempotent operations get an idempotency key generated once per user intent. Retries and re-submissions reuse the key, and the server (or a local unique constraint) dedupes. On cancel, I treat the outcome as unknown, and I reconcile by querying state by key instead of showing "failed".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Three outcome classes after a CE:

Where cancellation hit Side effect happened? What the client knows
Before the request was written No CE
After the request was sent, before the response Maybe (server often completes it) CE
After the work finished, before dispatch back (Q368) Yes CE

All three look the same from inside the coroutine. That's an at-least-once situation: users retry, so the operation may run twice.

Design tools:

  1. Idempotency key generated when the user taps, persisted with the draft (not regenerated per retry). Sent as a header such as Idempotency-Key. The server stores key to result for a window (for example 24 h) and returns the same result for repeats.
  2. Local unique constraint or INSERT OR IGNORE/upsert by key for DB writes, so a replay can't duplicate rows.
  3. Reconcile, don't assume. After a cancelled submit, the next screen loads the order by key. "Pending" or "Confirmed" is shown from state, not from the exception.
  4. Durable execution for must-finish work. Run it in an app-owned scope or WorkManager so screen exit doesn't abandon it midway (C7). Cancellation then stops only the waiting UI.
  5. Compensation when the operation can't be made idempotent: a follow-up cancel/refund call.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class CheckoutViewModel(private val repo: OrderRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private var draftKey: String? = null           // survives retries; reset only after confirmed result

    fun submit(cart: Cart) {
        val key = draftKey ?: UUID.randomUUID().toString().also { draftKey = it }
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.value = Submitting
            _state.value = when (val r = repo.placeOrder(cart, key)) {   // sends Idempotency-Key: key
                is Placed -> { draftKey = null; Done(r.orderId) }
                is Failed -> Retryable(r.reason)      // keep the same key
            }
        }
    }
}
// On CE we never show "failed"; the next open reads the order by key and shows its real state.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Generating the idempotency key inside the repository call. Every retry becomes a new operation.
  • Showing a failure dialog on CE and inviting a retry without a key (Q368 war story).
  • Assuming the server rolls back on client disconnect. Most frameworks keep running the handler.
  • Persisting the key only in memory. Process death mid-flight loses it, so persist it with the draft for payments.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the key protect against two different taps? → Only if both reuse the same key (same intent). Double-tap protection at the UI/state level is a separate concern (C8).
  2. How long must the server keep keys? → Longer than the client's maximum retry horizon, commonly hours to a day.
  3. What about idempotent GETs? → Safe to cancel and repeat. The concern is only writes and external effects like payments, emails and push sends.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "cancel the request and show an error". The senior answer treats cancellation as unknown outcome, uses idempotency keys scoped to intent, reconciles by state, and moves must-finish work out of the screen's lifecycle.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A food-delivery checkout double-charged about 0.4% of users on flaky networks: timeout, CE, user retries, a new request with no key. An idempotency key persisted with the cart draft dropped duplicates to near zero.

questions.contextHtml:
An offline-first notes app imports a 300k-row CSV on Dispatchers.Default (4 cores on the target low-end device). A code review added "responsiveness" by calling yield() after every row. QA now reports the import takes 41 s versus 12 s before. Users cancel the import often, and before the change, cancellation took up to 12 s to take effect (the loop had no check). Profiler: 70% of time in DispatchedContinuation.resumeCancellableWith and queue operations, with the parse and insert itself well under 30%. A teammate wants to remove yield() entirely. Another suggests delay(1) per row to "let the UI breathe".

suspend fun import(rows: Sequence<String>) = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    for (line in rows) {
        yield()
        dao.insertBlocking(parse(line))     // ~35 µs per row
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: How do you balance cancellation latency with throughput here?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Remove yield()" (cancellation back to 12 s), or "use delay(1)" (300k x 1 ms = 5 minutes minimum). Neither is measured.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What cancellation latency is acceptable? (Sets the check interval.) Is the UI actually janking, or was yield() added speculatively? Default is a background pool, and yielding isn't needed for UI smoothness. Do rows need individual transactions?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace per-row yield() with a time- or count-based check. It's a one-line change that restores speed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) yield() costs a dispatch round trip per call (about 100 µs under contention here, versus 35 µs of real work). 300k x ~100 µs is roughly 30 s of pure overhead, which matches 41 s - 12 s = 29 s.
    • (b) Per-row inserts without a transaction (each insert is its own fsync). That's a separate, bigger cost that was already in the 12 s.
    • (c) GC from Sequence and line allocation. Minor.
  4. How I'd verify each: Macrobenchmark or a simple timing harness comparing variants; the Android Studio CPU profiler or Perfetto flame chart (confirms dispatch frames); DebugProbes isn't needed. SQLite trace shows N transactions for (b).
  5. Root cause: yield() is a real suspension, not a flag check. It allocates a continuation path and re-dispatches. At 35 µs of work per iteration the overhead dominates. A volatile read, as in ensureActive(), costs nanoseconds.
  6. Fix: Batch the checks and batch the writes. 
    suspend fun import(rows: Sequence<String>) = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    val batch = ArrayList<Row>(500)
    var n = 0
    for (line in rows) {
        batch += parse(line)
        if (++n % 500 == 0) {
            ensureActive()                    // every 500 rows ≈ 17 ms of work → cancel latency ≤ ~20 ms
            dao.insertAll(batch)              // one transaction per 500 rows
            batch.clear()
        }
    }
    if (batch.isNotEmpty()) dao.insertAll(batch)
}
    At 500 rows per check and 35 µs per row, cancellation latency is about 17 ms and there are only 600 checks in total. Use yield() once per batch only if other Default tasks must get fairness. Making the DAO calls suspend and using @Insert suspend also gives a cancellation point per batch for free.
  7. Prevention: Put a benchmark in CI for import throughput with a regression budget. A review guideline: "checks cost nothing, yield()/delay are for fairness and cost microseconds each".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use delay(1) per row, which turns a 12 s job into 5+ minutes. I wouldn't drop checks entirely. I wouldn't move to IO to "fix" it, as the work is CPU plus DB.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is batch size 500 and not 5,000? → Cancellation latency scales with batch time: 5,000 x 35 µs = 175 ms is still fine for a cancel button but not for a 60 fps animation, which doesn't run on this thread anyway. Pick from the latency requirement, then measure.
  • Is a time-based check better? → Checking System.nanoTime() every row costs about 25 ns, which is fine, and gives constant latency regardless of row cost.
  • Does ensureActive() hurt throughput measurably? → In a loop of tens of microseconds per iteration, no. In a tight 5 ns-per-iteration loop, check every few thousand iterations.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A log-compaction job called yield() per record "for fairness" and ran 4x slower. After batching, it was within 3% of the no-check version, and cancel latency went from 40 s to 20 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: removes the check or adds delay(1); no measurement.
  • Hire: knows ensureActive() is cheap and yield() is a dispatch; batches checks.
  • Strong hire: quantifies overhead and cancel latency, also fixes per-row transactions, and states the fairness-vs-throughput rule.

questions.promptHtml: How does cancellation work when collecting a Flow? What happens to the producer when the collector is cancelled or stops early with first() or take()?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Flow cancellation is where coroutine cancellation meets cold streams. Misunderstanding it leads to leaked listeners and unexpectedly aborted collectors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A flow is collected in the collector's coroutine, so cancelling that coroutine cancels the flow. The producer's emit is a suspension point and throws CE, unwinding the flow {} body through its finally. Operators like first() and take(n) stop early by throwing an internal CancellationException subclass that aborts the upstream; they are cancelling this collection, not your coroutine. Flow builders check the Job on emit, so a flow that emits regularly is cancellable. A flow {} that never emits or suspends is not. And since a Flow's CE is a CE, catch blocks inside it can swallow it, and emit inside a catch-all can mask it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
collector coroutine ──collect {}──► flow { ... emit(x) ... } (runs inside the collector's coroutine)
    cancel()  ──────────────────────► emit(x) / delay() throws CE → flow body unwinds → finally runs
first():   downstream throws AbortFlowException (a CE subclass, internal) → upstream unwinds → first() catches it,
           returns the value. The collector's own Job is NOT cancelled.

Key facts:

  • flow {}'s emit goes through ensureActive() checks. flow { while (true) emit(i++) } is cancellable, while flow { while (true) { compute() } } is not.
  • With callbackFlow/channelFlow the producer runs in a separate coroutine inside a channel. Cancelling the collector cancels it, and awaitClose { } is where listeners are unregistered (C10 covers that fully).
  • flowOn introduces a coroutine and channel, but cancellation still propagates in both directions, and the upstream is cancelled promptly.
  • Catching CE inside the flow:
flow {
    while (true) {
        try { emit(load()) } catch (e: Exception) { /* swallows CE thrown by emit/load after cancel */ }
        delay(1_000)                  // throws CE again → at least the loop ends here
    }
}

It ends only because delay throws. With no further suspension, the loop could spin.

  • Exceptions thrown by emit's downstream (the collector lambda) propagate through the producer's try/catch. Catching them breaks exception transparency (F1/F6).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val job = scope.launch {
    callbackFlow<Location> {
        val cb = LocationCallback { trySend(it) }       // simplified
        client.requestLocationUpdates(request, cb, Looper.getMainLooper())
        awaitClose { client.removeLocationUpdates(cb) } // runs on cancel, first(), take(), or completion
    }.first { it.accuracy < 50f }                       // early stop → CE subclass → awaitClose runs
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• try { ... } catch (e: Exception) wrapping collect/emit and swallowing the abort exception, which makes first() hang or return wrongly.
  • Assuming a cold flow stops when the screen stops but its collector coroutine is scoped to something longer-lived.
  • CPU-only flow {} loops with no emission or check.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does collectLatest cancel the previous block? → Yes. When a new value arrives, the running block is cancelled with a CE. That's why blocks under collectLatest should be cancellation-safe and use NonCancellable for must-finish writes.
  2. Does cancelling the collector cancel the upstream viewModelScope work in stateIn? → No. stateIn(WhileSubscribed) runs upstream in its own scope and stops it when the subscriber count has been zero for the timeout (F5).
  3. What does onCompletion receive on cancellation? → The CE as cause, so it can distinguish normal and cancelled completion.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "cancel the collector and the flow stops". The senior answer knows the producer runs in the collector's coroutine, first()/take() abort via internal CE subclasses, flows need emission points to be cancellable, and swallowing CEs inside flows breaks both cancellation and exception transparency.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sensor flow's awaitClose was missing. Leaving the screen cancelled collection, but the listener stayed registered and drained battery. Android vitals showed 3x the sensor wake-up rate until the unregister was added.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app's article screen saves a "read" marker and prefetches the next 5 articles. After a refactor to "make saving reliable", crash reports and memory graphs changed: ANR rate rose from 0.15% to 0.45%, and heap dumps from OOM crashes (0.6% of sessions) show ArticleFragment instances retained after onDestroy. Leak path in LeakCanary:

┬ GC Root: Thread DefaultDispatcher-worker-2
├─ kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedContinuation
├─ ArticleViewModel$onLeave$1 (anonymous Function2, captures `this`)
├─ ArticleViewModel
└─ ArticleFragment.binding  → retained, leaking

The code:

class ArticleViewModel(private val repo: ArticleRepo) : ViewModel() {
    fun onLeave(article: Article) {
        viewModelScope.launch(NonCancellable) {          // "so it always finishes"
            repo.markRead(article.id)                    // 20 ms
            repo.prefetch(article.nextIds)               // 5 network calls, 2 s each on slow links
            _events.value = Event.Saved                  // StateFlow<Event?> collected by the Fragment
        }
    }
}

Red herring: the team also upgraded Coil in the same release.
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong, why does it leak and ANR, and what's the right way to make "mark read" reliable?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, NonCancellable ensures it finishes; the leak is Coil." That misses that launch(NonCancellable) removes the Job relationship entirely.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is markRead required to survive screen exit but prefetch not? Is the Fragment retained by the ViewModel (ViewModels shouldn't hold views, so what holds the binding)? Where does _events get collected?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix by removing NonCancellable from the launch, which restores normal scoping. Keep a short durable write for the marker only.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) launch(NonCancellable): the new coroutine's Job is NonCancellable, with no parent. It is detached from viewModelScope, so onCleared can't cancel it, and nothing waits for or tracks it. The 5 slow network calls run to completion even after the user left. A fast "leave" loop then stacks dozens of those coroutines.
    • (b) The captured lambda holds the ViewModel, and the ViewModel (via a collector or listener, and _events consumer wiring) keeps Fragment-derived references alive for the 10 s the coroutine lives. If the ViewModel is Activity-scoped, or if the lambda or repo callback captured the Fragment context, the leak path matches the LeakCanary trace.
    • (c) ANR: the stacked prefetches and decode work contend for Default/IO threads plus main-thread _events updates. Contention, not main-thread blocking, is the likely cause. I'd check main-thread stacks in the ANR traces before blaming it.
    • (d) Coil: possible for the memory story, but it doesn't explain the NonCancellable Job in the path.
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary trace (already shows a coroutine lambda as the retaining path). Add CoroutineName("onLeave") plus the debug agent and DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() to count live coroutines after leaving the screen 20 times. A test: call onLeave, call viewModel.clear(), and assert the coroutine's job is cancelled. It isn't. ANR traces from Play Console for main-thread state.
  5. Root cause: NonCancellable is a Job that is always active and has no parent. Passing it as the Job of launch replaces the parent link, so structured concurrency is gone. The coroutine isn't cancelled by onCleared, and nothing tracks it. Using it for the whole operation turns "cleanup that must finish" into "everything runs unconditionally".
  6. Fix:
    • Short term: scope it normally, and protect only the tiny durable write.
    fun onLeave(article: Article) {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        withContext(NonCancellable) { repo.markRead(article.id) }   // 20 ms, bounded
        repo.prefetch(article.nextIds)                              // cancellable like normal work
    }
}
    viewModelScope is cancelled when the ViewModel clears, but the markRead block still finishes if cancellation hits while it runs. If the launch itself is cancelled before withContext begins, the block won't run at all. That's fine for the screen-exit trigger (the coroutine started in onLeave), but for the guarantee, do it as a non-suspending enqueue or use the repository's app scope.
    • Long term: put must-finish writes in a repository that owns an application-scoped CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + ioDispatcher) injected by Hilt (C7), or use WorkManager for work that must survive process death (prefetch is optional, so skip it).
    class ArticleRepo(private val appScope: CoroutineScope, private val dao: ArticleDao) {
    fun markReadDurable(id: Long) { appScope.launch { dao.markRead(id) } }   // not tied to any screen
}
  7. Prevention: A lint rule or Detekt custom rule that flags launch(NonCancellable)/async(NonCancellable) (the docs say it's for withContext only). A unit test that clears the ViewModel and verifies no coroutines remain. A review checklist item: "NonCancellable only inside withContext, only for bounded cleanup".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I wouldn't use GlobalScope for durability, which has no cancellation or testing story. I wouldn't wrap the prefetch in NonCancellable to keep the ANR/leak away. I wouldn't treat Coil as the fix without evidence.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if markRead must never be lost even on process death? → Persist the intent synchronously (a Room insert in the same call, or a WorkManager OneTimeWorkRequest) and let a worker sync it.
  • Why does viewModelScope.launch(NonCancellable) still compile? → NonCancellable is a Job object, so it's a valid context element. The API doesn't prevent the misuse, which is why the lint rule matters.
  • Is withContext(NonCancellable) at the very start of the coroutine safe? → If the coroutine is already cancelled when it starts, withContext throws before running the block, because the check happens on the caller's context. NonCancellable only helps once you're already inside the block.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "save draft on exit" fix used launch(NonCancellable) and shipped. Two releases later, heap dumps showed hundreds of retained Activities after rapid screen switching, each holding a pending 30 s upload. Moving the write to an app scope with a one-slot queue fixed memory and cut OOM crashes by about two thirds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: says NonCancellable "makes it reliable" and blames Coil.
  • Hire: explains launch(NonCancellable) detaches from the parent, and narrows NonCancellable to a withContext around the write.
  • Strong hire: also explains the cancelled-before-start edge, moves durable work to an injected app scope or WorkManager, reads the LeakCanary path correctly, and adds lint/tests.
